entry.title: Thejesh Gangaiah Nagarathna
entry.content:
I have been thinking about writing about my full name for a while, especially after this incident in which an AI hallucinated my full name. Now that I have a post titled with my full name, it should help our future overlords!

Yes, my name is 3 first names. Mine, my fathers and mothers. Apparently, when I was being admitted to school, my mother was adamant that her name should be part of mine. Strangely enough, her colleagues (other teachers and the H.M.) discouraged it, not anyone else. But she persisted. So I got both of their first names in my name. As it was tradition then, they didn’t expand it. So it was only Thejesh G.N. until I got my passport.

For my passport, I had to expand the name. But it only had two columns, so “Gangaiah Nagarathna” became my surname name. It continued like that with my other official documents, though it’s not my surname and for some good reasons I don’t like the concept of surnames.

When I went to the US, they wanted a surname locally. For some strange reason, they want to call you by your last name. So I was “Mr. Nagarathna”. I have missed my name being called so many times. They have also called me “Mr. Thejesh G Nagarathna.”

Now that you know the story behind my name. My domain is actually my official name, “Thejesh GN”. For a long time, I used “Thej” as my online identity until Gmail came and didn’t allow 4 characters. So I moved to gnthej. After I got and moved to this domain in 2007, I started consolidating all my online identities under “ThejeshGN”. So today, most of them use that name; places I still use thej. I do still own and use thej.in.

Okay, as a technologist, I have issues with how names are handled online. I think the name should be a single text box with minimal validation. But for some reason, everyone online and offline wants to split it in some weird way or have some weird validations. Recently, I couldn’t add G.N as a surname for a flight; I had to enter GN. I don’t have to talk about folks having problems matching their names from PAN to Aadhaar or Voter ID. I recently saw a form where I had to enter “Thejesh Gangaiah” in the first-name column and “Nagarathna” in the last-name column.

We also decided to continue this issue for the next generation with “Uma Thejesh Anjana” :)

This post responds to an IndieWebClub/Bangalore prompt: What’s the story behind your domain name? (Or your government name, or your online handle.) I wasn’t there in person, but it was tempting.

entry.title: Outside is inside, inside is outside
entry.content:
Days are tough, nights painful.
I confront and suppress my fears,
Of what may happen to my dears

I catch myself worrying and frowning.
Tired of my own defaulting and fawning.

Even when I feel sure of what to do.
The right, nay, healthy thing to do.

Problem is, I’m not the right kind of right.
To do the right thing right now

I never know who is tormenting me.
The person outside or the one inside

Besides, tormented I am, regardless.
Stumbling to find my path to happiness

I see glimpses of it, I imagine it vividly.
But chasing it is too painful, repeatedly

I question my self, who it really is?
Is it one or selves, me or my parents?

Who is suppressing whom?
Who is pleasing whom?

Who is giving up autonomy?
Who is taking away agency?

Who am I really, am I really my own?
Such are my nights, anxious and sorrow.

entry.title: [Blog] What’s in a name?
entry.content:
> What’s the story behind your domain name? (Or your government name, or your online handle.) > This post is a response to an IndieWebClub prompt

My domain name is just my government name, Tanvi Bhakta. Tanvi means epitome of feminity - it comes from the root word tan which means body. But that’s not what my mother (who named me) told me :) She said that Tanvi means “of strong body and beautiful mind”. She said it is another name for Parvati, the wife of Shiva.

The story goes that Parvati, a princess, had decided she wants to marry Shiva (and Shiva alone). So she leaves the worldly comforts and climbs a mountain where very little grows and meditates, calling upon him, for days. Amused, Shiva takes the form of a tribal hunter and questions her desire - he says, “O you of such strong body and beautiful mind, what do you want with the likes of a man as crude and uncouth as Shiva?” She is affronted and defends her beloved well, winning him over and ultimately marrying him. It is from this shloka that my name was taken.

My surname, Bhakta, is not typical for the caste I belong to. Most surnames in the caste I belong to have been around for several hundred years - they are the Kamaths, Nayaks, Pais, Shenoys, etc. But apparently, my grandparent’s grandparents were very pious people. They undertook some kind of pilgrimage and established two temples - one off the coast of Kumta, and one in today’s Kasargod. For this deed, they were named “Bhakta” - the devotee.

Today, the word Bhakt is synonymous with an AndhBhakt - a blind devotee. It is (rightly) a pejorative. I used to think about changing my name but I can’t think of anything I would change it *to*. I have introduced myself with this set of syllables for too long now - it is a part of who I am; the syllables have almost lost their meaning as anything apart from my name. Thankfully, I’m able to separate the meanings in my head :)

[insert Ted Mosby calling a bowl a bowl gif]

I’ve also chosen the name Tanay for myself. It means *the chosen son*. Mum refuses to tell me now, but I think it might have been a contender for my name if I had been a boy? I like that it can play with lots of things - chosen by who? Me! Whose son? The son of *the chosen family*. Son? Or maybe Sun? (My favorite element). I like that it has a strong gendered aspect, to mirror my government name. Tanay Bhakta. It fits, and it feels like a version of me that could have existed.

For a long time, I went by the handle padawanjack. When people see it, they instantly make a Star Wars joke. I am sorry friends, I have never watched Star Wars (and I don’t intend to). When I had to come up with an online handle for some dumb site, I had a vague notion that Padawan meant student of some kind, and I thought that Samurai Jack was cool. I wanted to be perceived as a nerd of some kind, and I wanted to learn sword tricks and perseverance in the face of horrifying evil (Aku). Please cut me some slack, I was probably 8 years old and wanted to play flash games.

I also have another handle based on the characters but I’m not going to doxx myself with that one :grin:

Nominative determinism the theory that what something is named can predict what it becomes. I think names are indicative of a wish that the name-giver has for the named, and that can often be an indicator of the environment that the named grows up in as well. Names are often used as a tool for meaning making in the relationships they we come across later in life. Indian names are especially fun because some meanings are very on-the-surface and can be used in all sorts of puns.

I think I’m pretty bad at coming up with names, and it’s a skill I would like to get better at without thinking too much about the consequences.

---

Related: The story of roughly fifty Sanjanas, how their parents decided to call them that, and the secret history of why Indians give their babies the names they do; https://fiftytwo.in/story/the-namesakes/

entry.title: In search of the perfect media experience
entry.content:
One feed at a time.

The rabbit hole

A recent conversation in the IndieWebClub Bangalore (IWCB) WhatsApp group about RSS readers and reading habits sent me down a lovely rabbit hole. I found fun new apps, rediscovered a few old ones and, best of all, got a glimpse into how folks at IWCB read. Some of you have fascinating, occasionally hardcore reading habits. I am looking at you, Abhinav.

As I was thinking about everyone’s reading chronicles, I went back to my own RSS reader and felt oddly lost. My setup, which had been working fine for a year or so, felt broken. I was curious about different apps, new ways to organise my feeds and different ways to read. Damn you, neurodivergent brain!

So I ended up taking a fairly drastic step. For the first time in seven years, I have no RSS reader. I have completely stopped reading feeds for now and am letting blogs reach me as they may. This does not include the IWCB friends. I am still visiting many of your websites and reading your words. Sincerely.

Reading as a river

Here I am now, looking for the right RSS reader for this version of me. I know the perfect reader does not exist, but I am looking anyway.

There are some baseline things that I want from an RSS reader:

  • Works seamlessly across Mac, iPhone and iPad
  • Is customisable without becoming a second job
  • Has good UX (very important). I cannot and will not compromise on the joy of using good software.

But the key thing for me is how I want to read. I do not want my RSS feed to feel like another job, with a queue of unread items to clear. I strongly align with Oliver Burkeman’s philosophy of treating one’s reading list like a river that keeps flowing, and I can dip in for the things that catch my attention and let the rest flow past.

My universe

RSS is only one part of my media consumption universe. My MCU, if you will. Yes, I am calling it that now. The whole thing is my personal hellscape. As Bo Burnham puts it, you can get “anything and everything, all of the time”.

There is YouTube, podcasts and news, as well as books and magazines. In reaction to my internal RSS crisis, I ended up unsubscribing from most other media too. Here I am, trying to rebuild my perfect universe again.

Before this reset, this was what my other media consumption looked like:

  • Videos, mostly YouTube: the biggest time sink. I subscribe to what I like, save what I want to watch later, then try to remember to watch it and close the app.
  • Podcasts: my weak spot. I am a sucker for a good narrative, especially on evening walks, while cleaning the house or washing utensils. A good story gives my brain one place to go instead of running in 10,000 directions.
  • News: I follow half a dozen or so publications across general news, technology, sports and more. Of course, they all have their own apps too.

And this still leaves out the books and magazines I read nearly every evening. I may have a problem, folks. The problem is me.

One medium at a time

Until recently, I was using Reeder to bring all these sources into one experience. It did all the things I cared about. No counts, no pressure, just dipping into a river. Lately, though, switching between text, audio and video in one feed has started to feel disorienting. These different kinds of media probably need to stay separate and do their own jobs.

Videos will stay on YouTube; I cannot avoid that. I am also looking for the right podcast app, but that is a separate exploration and a post of its own. Suggestions are welcome!

News will stay news. No one can fix that industry.

A current I might follow

An RSS reader I have had my eye on for a while is Current, which ticks almost all my boxes. It is available on all the devices, has no unread counts, and lets me group feeds into focused streams called “Currents” (you guessed it). The idea of each stream as its own river feels uniquely aligned to what I want.

More than anything, I respect that it has a clear point of view about what an RSS reader should be. The fact that it aligns with my own point of view surely helps its case. I want to try it partly because of that, and whether it ends up becoming the right reader for me is another question.

There is one small hiccup though, Current costs ₹999 as a one-time purchase. I do wonder whether I could recreate the same experience with NetNewsWire.

Whichever app I end up with, I want to see whether I can open my feeds, read something good and leave without feeling behind. That would be a good enough reason to keep using it.

For now, this is me building my media universe again, feed by feed. RSS first. Next up, podcasts.

entry.title: [Weeknotes] Week of October 17th, 2026: Learning while working, todoist overwhelm, and annotated novels
entry.content:
I am simply declaring bankruptcy on the weeks before this. I am also posting this entirely from my phone; maybe this way I will be able to write more.

Work

A few weeks ago I finally figured out how to get the llm to teach me things in a style in which I can learn. Working with llms has been much better since then.

I also hope that I have figured out the balance of using llms without outsourcing my thinking to them. I am doing at least 5 times the output of the work I used to do (pre llm). But I've found that I can care about at most 3 things a day, before my brain gets very, very tired.

I'll have a post up soon about how we're doing evals and what I learnt from it!

Life

My to do list (literally, the app) had somehow become a mix of things I must do to survive + dumb things I don't want to forget. The rest of my everyday tasks stayed in my head. This week, i finally put all of those tasks down in the app too! Instant catatonia. I got so overwhelmed looking at all of it that my brain just started haphazardly picking up things to get done even if it wasn't as important. All my regular self soothing mechanisms were not working. I called a friend, diagnosed the problem, and made several views for myself so that I am seeing smaller sets things in my everyday. But it was a good lesson that I am really just a bundle of systems that work and coping mechanisms.

Last weekend was Maya Bazaar. Got there super late, missed lots of my friends, skipped quite a few performances, but I'm pretty happy that I spent most of my money on stalls belonging to trans folks, and then some rings haha.

Azan did a set in his living room. For his birthday last week he did a very long noodley set that I still have playing in my head. This set was "tighter" but I know he is hiding more songs in his back pocket. Want a soundcloud link.

The rest of the week has been quiet. Didn't even leave the house except for Tuesday dinner. Been sleeping at 8pm where I can and the body has appreciated it.

Health

Still in the flare that started mid August. Getting a little tired of it now. Go away. The last week especially I have wanted to move more, but have been afraid. (Iykyk) Would not wish chronic illness on my worst enemy. Okay wait, i have thought about who my worst enemies are (hint: people have been marching against them!) and maybe I would.

A friend has offered to spend quality time with a bottle of oil and my back. I also hope to play some football this week. Let's see.

Learning

Apart from the recall teach skill i programmed, i finally lost my patience and got a kannada deck made for Anki. I'm having more fun than I have had with it before.

Media Diet

Reading

I wanted something familiar but epic so I have been rereading The Locked Tomb series via this annotated doc. It's like having all the theories in one place outside my head. But using google docs on mobile especially for a big doc is so painful. Unfortunately a lot of the reading experience also comes from reading the comments left on the doc, so I'm stuck to that platform for now.

Listening

Been really enjoying the quiet jazz of Nala Sinephro, especially her Spaces 1.8. Thanks Azan! Jhene Aiko's Westside Whimsy feels like classic rnb, great afternoon listening but forgettable. Having lots of fun with Bangalore ka Potta, thanks Ashlesh!

entry.title: gridlockd?
entry.content:
For as long as I can remember, I've loved cars. I used to (and still) get excited when I saw a cool car on the road. It doesn't need to be fancy, fast, or expensive; it just needs to be cool.

Adult money is cool. You finally get to make your 12-year-old self happy by giving them everything they wanted. So eventually, it was time for a car.

But before that, motorcycles had entered the scene. I borrowed my dad's motorcycle in college, and had it some time after that, too. I used to take it everywhere. 50 meters from my class to the library? Yes. 500km to the closest beach? Also yes. Not too long after, I got my first motorcycle, which also came with me everywhere. A car was always in sight, but was always something for down the road.

I now call Bangalore home, also home to some of the planet's worst traffic. During my first week after getting my own "cool" car, I spent most of my time with it stuck in bumper-to-bumper traffic. Grid locked. This only reinforced my long-standing theory that motorcycles are the best way to get around this city.

But no, it was not just my love-hate relationship with city driving that got me here to gridlockd. Tron: Legacy has been my favourite movie of all time ever since I first saw it back in school. I would accurately describe it as a 2-hour-long music video for Daft Punk's score, and it also has a way of making you fall for motorcycles. Most of the story takes place inside the Grid - a digital frontier. I would describe it as a world that exists inside a computer. The Internet has always been a place for me, one that existed on the family computer, accessible only during sanctioned after-school time. This blog may very well be a place on the Grid.

I use public transport to commute to work these days, and I walk back home. While Bangalore is by no means a walkable city, I get by. Each form of travel has a way of making your mind work differently. On a motorcycle, you are just out there, using all your limbs and senses to travel. In a car, you are a bit more relaxed. You have music to keep you company. On a plane, you are dehydrated, and despite sharing one of mankind’s greatest inventions with a bunch of strangers, you go into your own shell – you sleep, or you consume media. But while walking, your brain does not really have much else to do. Your legs already know where to go and when to turn. Which leaves the brain to be bored, and do what it does best: think.

I guess what I am trying to say is, gridlockd is a space where thoughts and ideas that most definitely came from a time when I was not grid-locked can exist in the grid.

entry.title: Weeknote 42 2026
entry.content:
We are heading towards Black Mirror reality one day at a time. This week, I visited Majestic metro station for the first time since moving to Indiranagar. And I was greeted with this:

https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/1-yDu_bpatQ?mute=1

FUCK YOU BMRCL. There are ads already on metro trains, on stations, with big LEDs and tall posters and now you won't let passengers stand in peace right at the docking spot. Bengaluru metro is the most expensive metro backed by bonkers ridership numbers, and they still want MORE money!

Life

Navratri

Navratri is finally here! As someone born and brought up in Gujarat, I naturally LOVE navratri. And yes, I can go beyblade while playing Dodhiya 🕺. I was trying to explain my colleagues why I love playing Garba so much. It mostly boils down to the trance state you enter when you are already super exhausted from the repeated high energy steps. To me that is super addicting!

On the first day, I went to play garba in Whitefield. I attended the same event last year, but at that time it was organized in a much smaller space. The hall this time was easily 4-5X bigger! There were so many people and I had SO MUCH FUN! This was my photo and video from that day:

https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/hs_U0lQrThY?mute=1

On the second day, I went to super famous Palace Grounds. I was with a group of extended Gujju climbing gang. And since they were quick to pick up steps, I had a blast with them! The only sad part was whole event felt way too commercial, and that killed the whole vibe for me. I need traditional songs (zero bollywood DJ nonsense) and people who know the steps.

These organizers instead were selling dandiyas, had zero water arrangements and were having dance performances from third party groups till 10 o clock. They were also running a money scam in the form of forcing cash only payments for food and water. If you don't have any, they would give you cash by charging 5 rupees per 10 rupees of UPI payment!! This absolutely blew me away, I hate organizers of this group, same as the BMRCL money mongers. FUCK YOU!

After this horrible experience I wanted something non-commercial and hence decided to go to: https://www.instagram.com/sriblrnavratriutsavmandal/. This group has been organizing non-commercial traditional garba for 45 years! And oh boy, this did not disappoint. We did two artis as per the tradition, followed by live music by an old couple who seemed to enjoy singing more than participating in the actual dance. It almost felt like Lata Mangeshkar and R.D. Burman were alive again.

Event felt more like organized by families, for families, so you had breaks where children are getting free gifts, there's lucky draw, etc. But overall, this was the best place amongst all. I felt nostalgic for my hometown 🤧❤️. Would definitely support them by donating.

If you are reading this weeknote and interested in joining me, lemme know!

Interview

After the first interview rejection, I reached out to a company which has been keen on hiring me for a while. I prepared and had the interview last week. I think the interview went really really nice! And guess what, I got rejected AGAIN.

Life's in a pretty weird phase right now. Getting rejected from DSA interviews where I solved the whole question with all the edge cases, and then being put into PiP with unreasonable expectations cause someone stopped liking me is PEAK!

I am optimistic though. Let's see where life takes me :).

Blogs

This week was productive for blogging. I published a poem named Dazai followed by a photoblog on Ganeshotsav.

I wrote the poem after getting rejected from an interview I was so sure I would clear. I got rejected for silliest of the reasons and was pretty bummed by that. As for Dazai, if you have watched Bungou Stray Dogs or are a fan of Japanese literature, you would know 🫣. I even got some encouragement from Jatan for the poem which I am super grateful for 🙇.

Hopefully, I can continue the streak and publish a couple more drafts in the upcoming weeks.

Stretching

With Navratri fever ON, I have ended up staying up super late every single night. This has caused me to miss stretching every day :(. This weeknote is an embarrassment marker for me to get back next week!

Climbing

I missed climbing this Sunday again 😭. I have decided to stay put at home this weekend, so that I can chill and actually spend doing my regular weekend routine. So yeah, in next weeknote, you would see climbing update of upcoming Sunday too!

Tuesday

They made some changes to the black level 6 I had linked last week, so I sent it again and much much smoother this time. Soft or not, smoothness is always good to have!

I also spent a lot of time trying this red level 5 and finally managed to send it! Starting moves are just your average slab with the best advice being, trust your foot. But the last move...I am standing on a credit-card-thin hold and I have to put my entire body weight on it! I kept falling on that move for half of the session but I didn't give up and suddenly:

https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/NEsoLWeH_RY?mute=1

After sending this, I moved on to the only remaining level 6 in this set, which is this cool swing-coordinate-run-slippery-volume-jump-catch-hold move! It is super cool, here is a video of me attempting it:

https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/ObTPUJKM56A?mute=1

Thursday

I am SO HAPPY that overhang and cave got RESET, lessggooo!! This set was F-ing hard tho, I couldn't flash anything, not even level 3s 💀. Well, it was a slip up, but that definitely took away my flash on the pink 3. Level 4s too were really hard this time, it took me quite a few attempts to understand the best way to send these. Though I am not sad overall, cause...I sent a really hard level 5.

Again, this was a shouldery, grip strength plus lockoff testing route, which is kinda my style. Because it suited me, I was able to send the route in a couple of tries! But...but...those attempts, mannn, they took everything out of me. It was a super tiring route! I got so tired, that I have still not recovered, even two days later! 😭

After this, I wasn't able to project the remaining two level 5s. Hopefully I can make good progress on them on Sunday :).

Food

This week was breakfast testing week! Yash, Harsh, and I tried Amma and Appa Idli and Babai Tiffins.

Amma and Appa Idli

Idlis and vada were decent, unremarkable though. Dosas were cooked with super soft base and were kinda different, definitely in a good way. We really liked Chilli Chutney and Egg dosa. One thing which surprised me was for the price, portions were small. I would have expected a lot more from a roadside stall, but I guess it got struck by the Indiranagar shrinkflation effect.

Babai Tiffins

This is one place where I had been before and was a huge fan of! After this visit, I would just say, it's a good place, no longer bearing the charm it once did. Idlis, Vadas and Dosas were as good as they get, but I miss two things majorly:

  • dense peanut chutney
  • purple grape juice

Chinita

I had also ordered Paneer Pambaza Sandwich from Chinita for dinner on Thursday. And mann, I have never had anything SO BAD from Chinita. This one had SUPER DRY bread, to the extent it was impossible to keep thrusting it down the throat without a drink on the side (thanks to Diet Coke for the help). I am not ordering this ever again, back to my default order of Spinach and Caramelized Onions Rice Bowl.

Cheesecakes

I went out with a colleague to a cheesecake place he has been praising for a while. It's called Maison du Brownie & Cheese Cake. A super narrow shop, situated just a lane away from 12th Main Road. We had two unnamed cheesecakes, but we just pointed to and ordered. They were really good! Sweet fairy in me is happy! 🧚

Tech

Another reason for staying put at home this week, was attending IndieWebClub meetup! As always it was super fun to be there. Just one regret: I forgot to interact with people, I had loads of questions for Abhinav, Ankur, Tanvi, Abhigyan and Aeisha 😭. Instead, I was consumed by the fixes I was doing on my website. Blogs section now is an uncategorised list of blogs with titles and dates instead of just slugs. This went through a couple of iterations including adding two parallel sections, which I decided didn't look good enough to continue. I guess I will ask them the questions in a session after Nov 20?

And finally in today's bad software rant: Slack's search bar is a bit too slow I believe. I can type much faster. And by the time it loads the partial result from few milliseconds ago, I have already typed out the full thing. I also have a habit of pressing enter immediately after typing out my exact search query, and as the search bar is still stuck showing the old entries, I am always led into the wrong chat :(

entry.title: OpenAI DevDay Exchange Bangalore
entry.content:
Aren't we happy to be fed. A powerful corporation has turned its gaze upon us.

I went to Whitefield to attend OpenAI DevDay. It was at the convention center in Sheraton hotel. I can't remember how I got the invite, but I probably filled a form somewhere. It was an enjoyable metro ride. The light rain formed little streaks on the window that showed overcast sky of outer Bangalore. The soft hum, rain sounds and fuzziness of the station announcements was calming.

Everyone in the compartment had wireless earbuds on. It occurred to me how prevalent they are. Those who weren't staring down at their phones and peppering vertical thumb flicks were staring at their feet, listening to something through their buds. I once again tried (and failed) to pinpoint what makes it so unbearable for a person to sit with themselves. Why is everyone plugging themselves into the matrix.

Aren't we happy to be fed.

I reached the venue and registered. There were a bunch of Americans running the operations and queues, running around and doing all sorts of busy work. I noticed that the stage, camera, and sound was also handled by an all-American crew, probably one they brought with them everywhere. That must have been expensive. I thought of that one time Trevor Noah cancelled his tour in Bangalore because of how unhappy he was with the sound arrangements.

On this venue, the sound arrangements were excellent. The music was sleek and lo-fi. The tables were white, with clean typography. The stage itself shared that familiar Japandi look, with the white and wood and plants in the corner. It definitely felt like they imported the San Francisco aesthetic into Bangalore.

Aren't we happy to be fed. A powerful corporation has turned its gaze upon us.

It was crowded, maybe just an arm's length of free space around me at any given time. The crowds of young men (and the occasional woman) were concentrated in certain areas. Really, just three kinds of areas. The merchandise, the food, and this little backdrop to allow people to take photos to prove that they were there. The merch was fun, particularly the custom Codex pet cards. It seemed like someone could make their own design and get it printed on the spot.

I wasn't too interested in the food, and it all looked fried. I could smell the batter. I was happy to indulge in the coffee.

Aren't we happy to be fed. A powerful corporation has turned its gaze upon us.

There were a few booths from the various OpenAI teams, promoting the various things they were here to promote. I walked to the Dots booth, which is their personal always-on AI assistant. There was nothing in the booth, just a table. And two people on the other side of the booth from the Dots team. An absurd byproduct of this design was that a queue of people formed to make conversation with the booth people. I was standing behind this woman. When it was her turn, she started a conversation about how they are an MSME, and they have been experimenting with GPT Astra, their latest and most powerful model, to control a robot. She opened a video, and there it was. I saw a wheeled robot moving around and being controlled by the LLM.

The Dots guy was delighted, "Wow, this is amazing! Can I tweet this? Can you send this to me?"

He then offered to introduce this woman to a person in their team interested in hardware, and walked off the booth. He looked at me, somewhat apologetically and told me he'd be back in a few minutes, and he hopes I don't mind waiting. I enthusiastically thumbsed him up, as I genuinely did not mind. By then, the other Dots representative in the booth took me up on the conversation. I realised at that point I didn't really have anything specific or interesting to talk about. I joked about how it's funny that there's a queue for having a chat here, and I don't think it landed. I then asked a question about their Dots product, which was basically me trying to figure out why they announced @ChatGPT on Slack and Dots on Slack on the same DevDay, when the latter is basically a superset of the former. As anyone would imagine, it was a slightly lousy conversation. She was being nice, considering.

I later searched "OpenAI DevDay Bengaluru" twitter to see if anyone from OpenAI tweeted about the robot. I couldn't find it. The results were full of young men sharing screenshots of their DevDay emails proclaiming their delight in getting accepted into this event. One tweet said, "my GitHub commits got me here. now let’s see if my social skills can get me through OpenAI DevDay Bengaluru tomorrow 😶‍🌫️"

Aren't we happy to be fed. A powerful corporation has turned its gaze upon us.

The events were about to start. I took a second row seat. Next to me a young gentleman asked me if I had reserved the seat next to me. Of course not, please take the seat. He asked me where I'm from. I'm of this city, I told him. He said he had come all the way from Thiruvananthapuram. He was preparing for placements. He had an interview for this company set up in his city, and he showed me the JD. It is funded by Nvidia and Microsoft, he said. It's unclear what the interview round will be testing, and what tech stack and language I should prepare for. I told him that none of that matters anymore, perhaps unhelpfully to him at the moment. You see, the only thing that matters is how you are able to understand and break down a problem in front of you, it matters more in the long run than whatever Leetcode this company will ask. That's what you need to make it. He then asked me if he should focus on "core logic." Something about that framing frustrated me, but for the moment, I nodded.

I looked up that company later. I needed Claude to explain what they actually do, because the website was vague, obscure and full of cool-sounding jargon. It's a "deep tech" company from the US that basically puts tiny datacenters in huge shipping containers, so that defense companies, oil rigs, disaster management teams and the like can get fast compute at their site of operation. Their website had just rebranded to remove all mentions of "AI" and replace it with "SI" instead. They now have a subsidiary in India.

Aren't we happy to be fed. A powerful corporation has turned its gaze upon us.

The event on stage started. The managing director of OpenAI got on stage. He got everyone to woohoo them to prove their energy, and the crowd was happy to oblige. And then applauded the crowd for making it despite the rains, despite the traffic, and despite the journey to Whitefield. It was a fairly typical presentation for an event of this kind, especially in India. He talked about how India is the second largest "developer ecosystem" in the world (I agree, though I don't know what that means) and how 70% of cloud native developers were under 35 (I agree, though I don't know what that means) and how 96% of AI startups and developers rely on Open Source (I agree and I think I know what that means). OpenAI are positioning themselves as the more "open" AI, at least in the sense that they want to be the platform layer that enables downstream businesses and get AI in everyone's hands.

He then provided us an equation:

Impact=Opportunity×Competence×GritImpact = Opportunity × Competence × GritImpact=Opportunity×Competence×GritHe gave us stories about how a person was using Codex to label potholes, and automate submitting the complaints. He talked about a few prototypes people made for telemedicine, and how telemedicine can finally be solved, and implied we just need to figure out policy. There were some other examples. They have set up an ecosystem of "ambassadors" at the college level that will promote Codex, and help the builder ecosystem in India.

Aren't we happy to be fed. A powerful corporation has turned its gaze upon us.

The next one was from the CTO of Applications, talking about their massive DevDay releases that happened earlier in September.

The next one was a fun one, with two folks showing off the GPT Live API. The demo went pretty well. The crowd seemed to enjoy it.

I was not feeling it though. I walked out of the auditorium to get myself a cup of free chai.

Aren't we happy to be fed. A powerful corporation has turned its gaze upon us.

Another round of snacks came out. The crowds formed near them. A voice in my head was telling me to go back and read The Power Broker at home, instead of stay along till 8PM.

I did not eat any of the snacks. I realised I wasn't happy to be fed.

I left the gaze of this powerful corporation.1

  1. You bet I'm taking them up on the free ChatGPT Pro 100 subscription though. ↩

entry.title: My Personal Style
entry.content:
As I am growing older, I am interested in expressing my interests more as I move into the world, because it is an easy way to socialize (Like the proverbial gringo wearing the dragon ball z shirt in mexico hoping to stay safe of the cartel). This is something which is a challenge because that means I will have to figure out what my interests actually are.

So I took inventory of my many interests and hobbies and only some of them have clothing potential and they are:

  • Gaming

  • Anime and Manga

  • MMA

All three of these interests unfortunately have been plagued with low quality clothing and merch. This is unfortunate because when I was much younger and dumber I could be enticed by just pasting the logo of thing I love on a t-shirt with low quality acrylic and I would buy it in a heartbeat. I am sure some of you can relate.

Obviously now with my frontal lobes developed and as an adult with adult money I can engage in buying haute couture or what passes for that in these spaces anyway.

One brand which I would recco is Rush by Kira, their GTA vice city shirt is a very nice homage to scarface(It's a double homage because vice city itself is inspired by scarface? Feels more like a full circle moment), which I am wearing at this moment as I write (how meta!!) I also like their Cyberpunk Collection. Their t-shirts are high quality and don't scream "THIS IS MERCH" it's more like a knowing nod between ball-knowers.

For anything to do with sportswear or MMA, I would love to be in the income range to afford underarmor, but I will settle for Akiba because their rash guards have good designs which don't chafe your nipples and honestly when you are rolling around with sweaty men it's better to have your nipples unchafed. I would love to drop a couple of Gandhis on Venum because some of their designs are cool, maybe something I can consider buying for my birthday.

Anime merch is innundated with clothing which are low quality, often made by people interested in cashing in on the current new thing. This space needs to be much better than pngs slapped on a shirt and sent on it's way, given that the artists making art are inspired, I would hope that the clothes would reflect that.

I have been fortunate to run into vendors at Bangalore Comic Con who sold high quality heavy T-shirts which silhouette well and had good designs made my talented artists. Although for some reason their websites are inaccessible. Their loss honestly.

I also randomly came across a brand called ahankar which sells clothes inspired by Indian Mythological works. I think their designs are cool and bought two shirts which did get a good reception at a few social gatherings.

Kshm is doing some interesting things with their pants, which I would love to try out after getting to my goal weight and maintaining it because their pants look good on people with a much thinner waistline.

This is something which I have an opinion on. I think people with much better fashion sense can confirm this, Sometimes it's not the outfit it's the model. This has happened to me in my thick boy era where I would see buy sweatshirts which looked good on the catalogue but would look ridiculous on me, so now I judge most brands based on how their outfit would look on people who are large and incharge. Unfortunately, most brands will fail this litmus test.

I think my exploration with my clothing has just been finding interesting designs which don't get me weird looks because it looks not flattering on me. Outfits which silhoutte well are a must, I need heavy shirts which don't flap around in the summer breeze and pants which fit.

Honestly as long as it's not something with a bunch of logos dropped on it I don't mind buying cool looking Tees which are catching eyeballs.

entry.title: On Giving Up
entry.content:
Today in the drum class, I gave up playing the song I was practicing. I had already spent three days learning it, and still couldn’t play it properly. In particular, I couldn’t keep the right tempo. I realized that I shouldn’t try anymore, and decided to give up on it.

I am largely an autodidact in many interests of my life. I taught myself programming, reading music, running etc by reading books, watching videos, listening to people. A big part of learning by oneself is knowing when to give up. There are many things in my life that I’ve walked way from. Let me list a few2:

Playing video games
As I child I loved playing video games, but upon growing up I decided to stop. I realized that they were too addictive for me, and for the kind of person I am—even though they were a lot of fun—they were turning out to be a net-negative.

Higher mathematics
I scored a perfect 100 in Maths in my board exams (high-school exams). I loved solving all those deferential equations, and vector calculus, and what not. In college I tried but utterly failed in learning higher levels of Maths. I saw my limits, and I decided to not pursue it anymore.

Playing music
I’ve been playing drums on-and-off for a decade now. I won’t say I’m really good at it. I regularly try and give up on playing difficult songs. In fact, I have a playlist of songs for that. This resignation is different from the last two, because I know going in that these songs are too complex for me to play, yet I try. And often I return to them months or years later, and am able to play after a few rounds of failure.

The short list above shows that there are different methods of and reasons for giving up. I’m going to capture some that come to my mind:

Rest
Often you are too tired or overwhelmed to do something properly. In such cases, quit and try again in a few days.

Marinate
Some times things just don’t click immediately, but if you give yourself a few days/weeks/months of time to subconsciously digest the lessons of the failures, you may just be able to do it next time!

Step away
Some endeavours are simply too hard at your current skill/knowledge level. It makes sense in such cases to shelve them, and get better by doing/learning other unrelated activities. We don’t realize it, but often working on an unrelated strength may be the right choice at some points.

Give up
It is actually better to give up some things permanently. We all have limited time in our lives, and there is always a tradeoff between what you can do. Giving up on certain interests can in fact improve our overall lives.

I think it is okay to try and give up often than to never try at all. People grow and their lives changes. There is no reason to be stuck with something that doesn’t work for you. In fact, I suggest you give up profusely.

When giving up on purpose, it is important do it well. Think about why you are doing it, and if required, do a pro-con analysis. Talk to someone if you’d like to validate your feelings. Sleep over it in case you are confused. If you’d like to come back to it some day, make a note of it, along with your progress. Do not fluctuate between stopping and restarting again-and-again, stick to your decision. And finally, don’t feel guilty for giving up.

When I was writing this post, some folks suggested to just publish an empty post as a demonstration of giving up. That would really have been good fun, but it’s also equally important not surrender quickly for certain matters that are important to you. So here is to giving up or not—and knowing when to do which.

entry.title: The day I stopped singing
entry.content:
Exploring a creative wound.

This post was edited on 16 Oct, 2026[*]

I have a fairly deep voice. A voice that travels and fills a room. It is truly a joy using my vocal cords and feel them reverberate every time I speak.

Someone once told me that people pay attention when I speak, and that I should use my voice to that purpose more often. I never felt comfortable with that idea, and chose not to pursue it.

There is nothing wrong with people listening to me; I just had a different dream for my voice. I used to love singing. I still love singing, it is just slightly different now.

At school, I was part of the Indian music group, and music period was easily my favourite part of the week. Singing my heart out, I loved hearing my voice bounce around in that bright corner room of the school building.

Note on “Singing” · 16 Oct, 2026

i also tried learning the bongo, though that never progressed much beyond hyperactive teenage boy being given permission to bang on drums.

My Indian music teacher encouraged and supported my singing like no one else and deserves a special mention here. Unfortunately, I am forgetting her name right now, which is a terrible way to give someone a special mention.

But the seeds of my singing were truly planted at home. My dad used to play Kishore Kumar and Mohammed Rafi cassettes every morning, and I would sing along. As far as I was concerned, these were the best songs there had ever been, and loved singing them. In the infinite wisdom of youth, I imagined I would only get better at singing those songs.

Note on “best” · 16 Oct, 2026

this still holds true today.

And then the worst thing that could happen to my singing aspirations, happened. I hit puberty. My voice grew deeper and coarser and could no longer carry the songs that had brought me so much joy. Cracks had appeared in my voice, and the notes were leaking out.

For the first few weeks, I was completely thrown off. Losing a big part of my identity, teenage me had no idea what to do about it. I tried changing the songs. Kailash Kher became a favourite. His songs gave my increasingly coarse voice somewhere to go. Then it was Sukhwinder, Rabbi Shergill, and an optimistic attempt at Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan.

Note on “Kailash Kher” · 16 Oct, 2026

fun fact: he used to live two streets down from my house and taught music at a neighbourhood school.

But I was grasping at straws. My voice was changing faster than I could learn and adapt to new genres of music.

The turning point came in ninth standard, during auditions for an inter-house music competition. The teacher doing the selections was not my regular music teacher. She seemed surprised that I sang at all and dismissed my audition with little encouragement.

That memory still stings. I shed a few tears that day, much to the surprise of my friends. They did not seem to think it was a particularly big deal. It was for a kid whose entire life was filled with singing.

My Indian music teacher, realising I had not been selected, assumed there had been a mistake and asked me to join. I was grateful to join, but my voice was sticking out like a sore thumb. Two days before the competition, the other teacher who had rejected me earlier stopped by during a practice session and thought the sound was a little off.

To find out why, she pointed at me and asked me to sing alone. As my cracked voice came through, the whole group looked at me with horror. She asked me to stop, then had the rest of the group sing without me. After hearing the group, she asked me to leave.

My house went on to win the competition. If I ever needed a signal that the sun had set on my singing ambitions, this felt fairly unambiguous. The timing could have been kinder, though.

My love for singing endures even today. I sing by myself, and sometimes around people I am close to. But I have not let my voice loose the same way I used to in nearly two decades.

Somewhere along the way, I became careful with something I had never had to think about before. While I like my voice now, I am curious about what it would feel like to give it a little room again.

I think of Kailash Kher again, and of “Allah Ke Bande” the first song I turned to when my voice began to crack.

“Toota toota ek parinda aise toota, ki phir ud na paaya…”
A bird was shattered, shattered so badly that it could never fly again…

“Loota loota kisne usko aise loota, ki phir ud na paaya…”
Who robbed it, who plundered it so completely that it could never fly again…

“Girta hua hoon aasmaan se, aakar gira zameen par…”
Falling from the sky, it came crashing down to earth…

“Khaabon mein phir bhi baadal hi the, woh kehta raha magar…”
Yet clouds still filled its dreams, even as it kept saying…

“Ke Allah ke bande hans de, Allah ke bande, Allah ke bande hans de…”
O servant of God, smile… O servant of God, just smile…

“Jo bhi ho, kal phir aayega…”
Whatever happens, tomorrow will come again…

I will go try that now.

entry.title: Why I don't get annoyed at honking or Manu Joseph
entry.content:
There's a genre of complaining that's popular online, that talks about how everything sucks in India. There's a whole lot of you out there. I'll only punch up and say this article by Manu Joseph is the kind that I'm speaking of.

I am sympathetic to these views. It's worse for those with less economic and social privileges, and definitely downright unlivable for some.

However, I am only addressing the privileged Manu Joseph class of people, who have money and cushy well-paid jobs (often in tech), and who might be curious about why I don't get (persistently) annoyed at all the honking, garbage, wrong side riders, and our supposedly filthy, uncivilised society.

My underlying principle simple. Accept that you have the life you have. Make tradeoffs. The counterfactual life you are supposedly missing out on isn't real, and complaining about not having it is thus absurd. Everything is easier with this mindset, even in "hard-mode" India. All my solutions to being generally happy and not bitter in India comes down to me making tradeoffs. I find a lot of satisfaction in solving problems under constraints, and India can be a great playground for that.

Honking, traffic, pollution

For honking, I solved it for the most part by buying earplugs. I have these which come with a nice tiny pouch you can add to your keychain. I use these when walking around loud traffic areas.

For traffic, I solved it by living close to work (and "leisure") and living near a place with some metro connectivity and public transport. I don't drive. Where connectivity is sparse, autos suffice.

For pollution, my area happens to be relatively low AQI, but perhaps still not fantastic over the long term. For now, I have accepted this tradeoff, but I know that I have some options in the future like investing in masks and air filters.

Small annoyances

In India, you are subject to many small annoyances, like honking, pollution, uncivility, or Manu Joseph's substack. Just two days ago, I had to cross a flooded road because it rained earlier. I waded through the water. When I got home. I put my socks in the washing machine. And washed my feet. And I moved on and didn't think about it, except for now, in order to supply an example here (so perhaps this "annoyance" was a net positive?). I didn't have to internalise or tie it into a larger narrative of how my life is miserable for having to deal with these annoyances day in, day out.

I sometimes feel I get judged for talking like this, as though I'm endorsing that we not fix issues at the root, or we "just deal with it" instead of wanting change. This is not what I am saying. What I'm saying is that I'd rather be happy, and thus effective as a person, and this is more in our hands than most people assume. I strongly believe that one has to climb their own "Maslow" ladder so that they can start improving and looking out for others.

entry.title: My Favourite Art from October 10

“October 10” here refers to the entire (still ongoing) period of the SIR protests. If you aren’t informed yet, you can read more on Wikipedia and watch (my GOAT) Samdish’s video. ¶

This collection was originally much larger than it is right now, but I learned that a lot of the posts I saved have been taken down since under the State’s rigorous banishing of free speech online. You can read the Internet Freedom Foundation’s coverage on this. ¶

They ironically call it “enhanced diligence”, which is something they could have shown when crimes of rape and abuse became rampant all across the country. ¶

“हमारा ठोकरों से कुछ पुराना ख़ास नाता है।
है जिसने इश्क़ ही देखा ना, वो रब का दुलारा है।”

– Taare by Farak

“In order for me to write poetry that isn’t political
I must listen to the birds
and in order to hear the birds
the warplanes must be silent.”

– Marwan Makhoul

Some of this artwork might involve AI use. I don’t mean to demean real artwork by putting both in the same space; I appreciate real effort and skill achieved through hard work, and the toil that artists put into every single piece. But I also think everyone in a democracy has the right to dissent, and excluding alternative forms of expression at a time like this would be neglectful of me. ¶

I don’t know, my stance here is still a work in progress. But I find all exercising of our freedom of speech and expression cool as hell. ¶

entry.title: (#2026-W41) ikea, air conditoning and hope
entry.content:
The workdays felt extremely long this week. ¶

A lot of non-coding tasks lined up and joined forces with a deadline. I’m not particularly against documentation — I quite like it in fact, since I like to write — but reaching the finish line definitely felt slower than it does for programming tasks. I most likely have just gotten used to the speed of LLM’s though, which is a scary thought. ¶

In other news, I met a batchmate from college who just started interning in the same company. We bumped into each in the cafeteria and kinda went, “You look familiar,” and our current assumption is that we must’ve seen each other on LinkedIn or somewhere else. We caught up on our life events and placement shenanigans since college, and my cafeteria breaks passed by a little bit faster. ¶

Walking around the tech park after lunch has made me think a lot about air conditioning recently. ¶

I see these huge office buildings, their rooftops brimming over with AC units and backup generators and even some solar panels. Going to any balcony close enough to them will have you witness a low and consistent hum all throughout the day. Heaps of heat constantly dissipating from the tops of these buildings. ¶

I remember going to Goa and looking at the shape of a beach on the map; how a small “C” shape on the screen was a really big area in-person. And as I realize the scale of the Earth more and more, and see the collateral from a single building, I keep thinking, “We must really be hurting the Earth for it to be getting worse.” ¶

I start thinking about the landfills and the water pollution, the factories and the data centers. All of the hurt and neglect stacking up. I spend some time in that hopelessness, before a coworker taps me on the shoulder and asks me if I want ice-cream. ¶

Bangalore weather has reached that weird point where I can’t figure out whether to sleep with the fan on or off. It gets too cold by the time I wake up, and I have to do the healing shenanigans for a scratchy throat/runny nose. ¶

Afternoons still seem pretty hot though, with the Sun blazing over any part of the tech park not covered by tall glass structures. The fluctuation is weird. I saved a meme in this context, that I’d like to share here: ¶

“its 85 degrees in october because you guys can’t stop asking chat gpt to make y’all fuckass flyers”

Is it really a meme if it’s true? ¶

News around the SIR protests gained volume towards the end of the week. Visuals of brutality and censorship made their rounds on the social media algorithms in the thousands. A close repetition of the events from the NEET protests in July, except you could tell the State was more prepared this time. ¶

When I last wrote about the NEET protests, I remember being in despair over the treatment towards the students. I kept track of the events from afar, and even reposted reels and the like on my Instagram Stories; I’m not sure why, but most likely to find solace in sharing what I was seeing with everyone else. ¶

I remember feeling intense relief when the resignation of the Education Minister was finally announced. “They’d won,” was how I thought about it back then. The feelings have gotten more mixed since then, which is something I have written a bit about (but that draft is still rotting unpublished). ¶

Anyway, I had all this floating around in my head when I went for a swim with Marathi Gang, and the conversation in the cab afterward volitionally turned to the events of the SIR protest. ¶

There was (surprisingly) much doubt and pessimism around the effect of the protest and its ability to actually mitigate the “root cause” of the current power situation. I shared my thoughts and we all had a healthy back-and-forth. I’ll gloss over the details of the discussion, but what I learned at the end is that I was actually hopeful about the future of it all. ¶

Once again, I really wish my draft for this was already up. But I believe the actual “victory” of the Cockroach Janta Party protests was that they started a chain of dissent. They showed people that they can get up and say “No, you cannot treat me like this. I’m not an inanimate metric on your tenders and flyers. I’m a living, breathing citizen.” ¶

The people who had tolerated bad policies and procedures could now feel connection, could see that there are other people facing the same “bad” and are not happy about it. They’re now giving themselves the permission to speak up. They’re allowing themselves to say, “No, you cannot treat me like this. I get hurt by your political neglect and feel sorrow when people around me get hurt by it too.” ¶

There’s a lot of pent-up rage flowing through the masses and their actions right now. All of it understandably so. The State might be able to summon enough lathis today to try and curb it all, but over time they will have to admit their faults and change. And, in the long run, it is us that will form the next wave of leadership. It is us who will use the coffers full of our tax money to bring the progress we were promised. We will do all that, pinky promise. ¶

Now don’t be mad, but this was my first time having food at Smash Guys. And I’m shook by my own neglect of this place. The food was so good (and so filling) that I had to stare at the ceiling once I was done just to recuperate. I noticed similar reactions from the rest of Marathi Gang. ¶

I probably should experiment with going to more new eating places (by which I still mean the well-tested ones). I’m yet to go to Paris Panini, for example. And I didn’t go to Corner House until a couple years ago, even though I’ve been in Bangalore for a little over four years. There seem to be many new things to try, and that’s always exciting. ¶

Once we finished our food, we got into the metro and began our looong journey to reach Ikea for some friends that were furniture-shopping. ¶

It had been a couple years since I last went to Ikea in Bangalore; reaching it is no easy feat anyway, since it’s over an hour away from Indiranagar. But the big blue warehouse and the layout inside was almost exactly as I remembered it. ¶

We first got a (non-alcoholic!) beer from the restaurant, and then began our journey of loitering around in the Ikea Showcase. We tested out multiple sofas and cooked a lot of khayali pulao around our future home interiors. At one point a grandma saw the bottles we were holding and gave us a bombastic side-eye, so we promptly started looking for a dustbin for the beers. ¶

After a swim, a heavy lunch and a long travel, going through the bedroom section of the Ikea Showcase was probably not a good idea. I remember sitting down on a bed and thinking, “Well, I can’t get up now.” We looked for the most uncomfortable bed we could after that, to sit down and plan our escape route to our intended shopping interest. ¶

After another 30 minutes of stumbling through the showcase to reach the Lighting section (and taking picture of things we found cool along the way), we learned that the one thing a friend wanted to buy was out of stock. Once the rep helpfully pointed out that we can order it from the website, we trudged along to the second restaurant for a break. ¶

We had our (unlimited refill!) drinks and chocolate croissants. We went out to the sign, took pictures, and started to leave towards the metro entrance. On our way out, I spotted the pillar where my school friend had crashed her cart the last time we were here, and that made me smile. ¶

I took the long metro ride home and that, my lovely readers, is where this weeknote ends. I missed out on Maya Bazaar this weekend due to other plans and general energy level, but I hope I can attend it next time. So many things to look forward to. ¶

Peace and love. ¶

entry.title: Did You Hear About the 100 Minors Who Died in Violence on October 10?
entry.content:
Rolf Dobelli wrote an essay in 2010 titled “Avoid News” with some 15 reasons why news is bad.

The number one reason is the most important. I quote a part of it:

News misleads us systematically

News reports do not represent the real world.

Our brains are wired to pay attention to visible, large, scandalous, sensational, shocking, people- related, story-formatted, fast changing, loud, graphic onslaughts of stimuli. Our brains have limited attention to spend on more subtle pieces of intelligence that are small, abstract, ambivalent, complex, slow to develop and quiet, much less silent. News organizations systematically exploit this bias.

News media outlets, by and large, focus on the highly visible. They display whatever information they can convey with gripping stories and lurid pictures, and they systematically ignore the subtle and insidious, even if that material is more important. News grabs our attention; that’s how its business model works. Even if the advertising model didn’t exist, we would still soak up news pieces because they are easy to digest and superficially quite tasty.

The highly visible misleads us.

By any estimate, at least 100 children die of tuberculosis in India every day. That is only tuberculosis.

These 100 children are victims of violence. Violence of kinds we don’t even call violence.

On October 10, at least 100 children died due to violence.

On October 11 too.

On October 12 too.

Every day in the past many years and in the coming many years these deaths will continue.

Our brains are wired to get emotionally provoked when we see violence plays out in very physical ways — like someone hitting someone. The more gore it is, the more violent it is, for our brains.

Most news outlets and algorithms are designed to amplify what our brains are wired to see — immediate emotion-evoking events.

But a lot of the violence in our society is not so visible to the untrained eye — caste, gender, capitalism, elitism.

This violence take the shape of physical assault, sexual assault, verbal assault, forced homelessness, forced landlessness, forced hunger, forced drinking of contaminated water, forced eating of unsafe food and nutrition-less food, forced breathing of polluted air, exclusion from schemes, exclusion from employment, underpayment, discrimination, exclusion from urban design, exclusion from public transport, hostility from healthcare system, hostility from education system, hostility from police, hostility from judiciary, hostility from bureaucracy, forced exposure to unsafe working conditions, forced exposure to unsafe work, forced work, forced lack of rest, forced choices, forced relationships, forced co-existence with unsafe people, parental neglect, social neglect, intergenerational trauma, exclusion from friendships, exclusion from opportunities, exclusion from desires, exclusion from dreams, and so on….

These rarely become news.

Even when these do, these rarely get noticed.

Even when these get noticed, these rarely get inside public consciousness.

Even if these are inside public consciousness, these rarely get addressed collectively or even individually.

In Manufacturing Consent: The Political Economy of the Mass Media, Edward S. Herman and Noam Chomsky apparently describe how media “carry out a system-supportive propaganda function, by reliance on market forces, internalized assumptions, and self-censorship, and without overt coercion”. They speak about factors like profit orientation that indirectly (or directly) make mass media automatically create an environment where certain ideas become truths.

I am making a more fundamental allegation against our society. I’m saying that content-creation of any form (including the so-called “independent media”, individual content creators, podcasters, bloggers, whoever they are) is influenced by similar incentives to cater to the biases of our social brain.

Even when advertisers and money are not in play, content creation is influenced by engagement. Content that receives less likes and shares are systematically discouraged. At least unconsciously, there’s encouragement to create content that gets more reach.

And as a rule, content that showcases high levels of drama will get more engagement.

This seems fundamental to how human brain works.

As long as some people are willing to game that, they will get more engagement. And engagement is limited. There are only so many viral videos that can be there in a day. So, whoever doesn’t play the game will be left behind. They’ll lose engagement, they’ll lose audience, and eventually they’ll lose motivation.

This means, that there is an underlying tendency in our society that corrupts all content creators.

How to fight this corruption?

Content creators need to pledge to themselves that they won’t fall prey to chasing the hype. They need to have a vision and they need to work towards that.

Content consumers need to pledge to themselves to introspect on their consumption habits. They need to actively question their biases. They should pause in the middle of scrolling sessions and see what they’re consuming. They need to be intentional about what they consume. They should compensate for their biases by actively seeking out less engaging, more important content.

All of us need to promise each other that we won’t encourage gaming our psychology. We should promise ourselves that we won’t fall into the trap of letting everyone else change before we change ourselves.

It is not going to be easy. But it is necessary if we want a fairer world.

entry.title: Getting Started with Reticulum
entry.content:
I have been looking for a network protocol stack that can be run in addition to the regular TCP/IP network at TVC. Kiran has been exploring Meshtastic, mainly to connect the sensors to the Home Assistant that TVC runs. We have very poor cell phone connection and two BSNL wired internet connections, one of which is mostly down. Kiran has been laying OFC across TVC to share that network. I took a bit off-route and started looking for a protocol that can work in adverse conditions; I was okay with high latency and extremely low bandwidth. Reticulam doesn’t make the OFC and network that is already setup at TVC. It works alongside TCP/IP, including over existing internet connections.

Reticulum is the cryptography-based networking stack for building local and wide-area networks with readily available hardware. Reticulum can keep operating even in adverse conditions with very high latency and extremely low bandwidth.

Unlike Meshtastic or MeshCore, Reticulam is not a messaging platform (though you can add messaging on top of it). It’s a full replacement networking stack. You can have many applications on top of it once it’s running. Ordinary TCP/IP applications do not automatically run on it.

In Reticulum, every machine or node is identified by a pair of signing and encryption keys (transferable). I fact a machine can have more than one. This is used for both encryption and routing. Both key pairs use 32-byte keys. Together, the two public keys form a 64-byte public identity. But to identify the node, Reticulum uses an identity hash, which is derived from these public keys.

hash = SHA256(encryption public key + signing public key )
identity_hash = first_16_bytes(hash)

That is 128 bits, or 16 bytes, or 32 hex characters. This is what you usually see everwhere to identify the node.

To route the traffic, Reticulum uses a destination hash, which is an address of an application endpoint in Reticulum. So different applications within the same node get different destination hashes. A normal identity-backed destination is derived from:

  • Application name, such as lxmf.
  • Aspects that identify the service, such as delivery.
  • Identity hash, identifying the key holder.

lxmf is a messaging protocol built on top of Reticulum.

name_hash = SHA256(b"lxmf.delivery")[:10] # First 10 bytes
destination_hash = SHA256(name_hash + identity_hash)[:16]

For rncp (file transfer utility like scp), the destination name is rncp.receive:

  • Application: rncp
  • Aspect: receive

The calculation is similar:

name_hash = SHA256(b"rncp.receive")[:10]
destination_hash = SHA256(name_hash + identity_hash)[:16]

This is how different applications on the same node can have different destination addresses. Packets are delivered to these destination addresses.

Applications can send an announce for their destination. An announce includes the destination’s public identity information and a signature that others can verify. As it travels through the network, nodes learn which direction that destination can be reached from and how many hops away it is. If a node does not know a path, it can request one.

Reticulum uses Transport nodes to carry traffic between other nodes, sometimes across different interfaces. Not every node needs to be a Transport node. Ideally a stationary, always on and available nodes can be a Transport node. A network needs relatively small number of Transport nodes.

Reticulam doesn’t have IP addresses, DNS names, etc. Everything is handled by cryptographic keys or hashes. Traffic is also encrypted end-to-end. All encryption keys are ephemeral, and communication offers forward secrecy by default. All of this is handled at the network level, and you don’t have to do anything as an application developer. The Reticulam protocol doesn’t support store-and-forward; the packets will be dropped if the destination couldn’t be reached or is down.

The network can use available mediums (like links, called Interfaces) to ship the packets. Your network can be heterogeneous based on your design. It can use SerialInterface (RS-232/485 line, serial radio modem, or XBee-style transceiver), PipeInterface (pipes packets through stdin/stdout), Internet (TCP), Local LAN, Ethernet or WiFi, automatically using IPv6 multicast. Bluetooth or other radio (LoRa, VHF/UHF/HF using KISS, AX.25 ), etc. Basically, it can use any medium as long as they transmit packets. You can configure more than one interface.

To get started, we will install rnsd (Reticulam Network Service Daemon). I installed it using UV, you can do pip if you want. It will install the rnsd and other utilities. Once installed, run rnsd to create a key pair. It usually creates a key pair in your home directory at ~/.reticulum. All your network keys are stored here. You can also edit ~/.reticulum/config to add interfaces. It comes with AutoInterface for local LAN/Wifi connectivity. But you can add one or two TCPClientInterface so you can send packets across the internet. You can start with an Interface provided by the community. It’s the easiest Interface to set up. If you change the config at any time, you need to restart RNS.

# using pip
pip install rns

# using uv
uv tool install rns

# run rnsd to create keys
rnsd

After that, you can create a system service if you’d like to run it as a service. I want it to run all the time, so I set it up that way. If not, you can start it manually whenever you want. You can check the status and traffic flow using `rnstatus`. It should show the status of all Interfaces and the traffic flowing through each one. Now you are on the network and ready.

To test you can pickup a node on Rmap, like this and see the path to it by running the command.

rnpath 5ee1bfcf91d35528c9dc22c083ea0594 # destination hash

It will print.

Path found, destination <5ee1bfcf91d35528c9dc22c083ea0594> is 7 hops away via 
<d7db22f63b453c23bb0688dde565b7c1> on BackboneInterface[PSHP G01/dyn1.intatec.com:4242]

Now you know you are on the network and can reach others on the Reticulam Network.

Next, install a useful app that can do something on this network, perhaps short messaging?

entry.title: Ganeshotsav 2026
entry.content:
Ganeshotsav is a 10-day festival celebrated in praise of Lord Ganesha, a Hindu god worshipped for his powers to remove obstacles. His presence is considered auspicious. And hence rituals worshipping him are performed before the start of any new venture for e.g. marriages, housewarming, new business, construction, etc.

During this festival, devotees all over India create pandals (makeshift bamboo encasements) with various themes and sculpt Ganesha's matching statues. It's always super fun hopping from pandal to pandal getting repeatedly stunned by devotees' creativity. This year's edition of the festival was celebrated from 14th to 23th September 2026, and I was in my hometown for a day to enjoy the festival. To give you an idea of the scale of celebration: I spent 6 hours in a single evening walking through tightly packed lanes in a small radius of 500 m. And that wasn't enough to cover all the pandals in that area! This is a minuscule part of the city. Imagine the number of pandals whole city would have!!

This photoblog is a collection of few of the pandals I liked where photography was allowed:

Outside a pandal, a Marathi band was performing. Their energy was super infectious. I was almost dancing the whole time. Look at their enthusiasm, endurance (they had already been performing for an hour) and coordination, it was super awesome!!

entry.title: Signs of the Times
entry.content:
Over years, I’ve been taking photos of random signs that I find interesting. I’m throwing some of them together in this note to create some sort of photo-note.

This post was originally published on abhinavsarkar.net.

First my favourite kind, the cautioning ones:

Asphyxiation is a nightmare thought to me. I’m not sure why they have spaces with hazardous atmosphere in a workplace, but I’m glad they put a big sign. Rest of these photos are also taken in my office, except the radiation warning one that I took in a hospital. Skull and bones signs are my all-time favourites. I like that someone decided they should err on the side of safety and put a “DO NOT DRINK” sign on a garden tap.

Next up, some vaguely threatening signs:

I like how they put GOD in quotes, and scatter shouty capital words in the top-left/first sign. When I took this photo, there was no car parked in front of their gate, so I guess it works, at least sometimes.

The folks from Bengaluru may know where the right/last sign is from. The top-left/first sign in Hindi translates to: “Stealing flowers from the park to offer them to gods is a sin. Do not be a sinner.” I hope the sign works; I’d like more flowers in the park.

Finally, some confusing signs:

The top-left/first sign reminds me of deprecation comments for functions that have been removed. “grandsfam accelefation” is a true mystery. No one knows what it means or where it came from. All searches about it only throw up these verbatim signs. The “Dept. of Computer Science” sign pointing to an abandoned building may really be the most prescient of all the signs on this page. I took that photo almost 20 year ago!

That’s all I have for this post. I hope it gave you a chuckle, or a nervous fright, or both.

entry.title: lifts and stuff
entry.content:
I am usually chill. The world moves through me without much trouble.

That said, in my head, I notice about a hundred subtly "incorrect" or subtly broken things in the world. I am secretly the biggest nitpicker, and this is a view into that part of my mind.

The lift

My apartment's lift has capacitive buttons. Capacitive buttons don't have a tactile feel, but the implications are beyond the dissatisfaction of calling the lift. Old people struggle to figure out how hard to press, and the feedback is not immediate. The press detection is unreliable.

The blind can work with physical buttons, as they can feel the grooves and edges. There could be braille too. But every button inside and outside this lift is behind a flat glass panel, and so there's no clear marker for them.

The doors of the lift also close after 30 seconds, in an apartment with extremely low footfall. Most people assume the doors don't close, and have to press a manual door close capacitive button every single time, every single day.

The software

Nearly every software or app I use requires a novel-sized book each if I were to list down the problems I run into. To put it in very broad categories, the issues are often:

  • The app doesn't actually succeed in its basic functions about half the time

  • The app is extremely slow and unresponsive

  • The app behaviour is surprising

My experience of using software lines up with Dan Luu.

Chairs and tables

I used to work out of an expensive WeWork. The chairs and tables are awful. They fail at basic ergonomics. The backrests of their chairs are arched badly and the tables are too high for most people of Indian proportions. They pretty much guarantee chronic back issues.

Dealing with it

Most of these problems have some useful levers for dealing with it, and I have made use of them to the extent I can.

  • Lift: Not done much about this, probably the hardest to fix. But when I see an old person (there's an old couple who lives upstairs) I operate around the quirks of the lift, so that it's less jank. If it's just me, I take the stairs, it's better for my health anyway.

  • Software: I avoid using features that don't work well, or I have developed some habits and workarounds (like copying text as I type it, instinctively hitting save). In general though, my software use for personal things is light. At work, there's probably little I can do, if the organisation has chosen bad software.

  • Chairs and tables: We bought our own chairs and tables, which solved the problem.

I am starting to realise that I am likely happy to be the person "dealing with it" so that other people eventually don't have to.
