entry.title: thoughts on negative outlooks
entry.content:
Abhinav prompted me to write about nihilism. The reason for this is likely because I end up having an "optimistic" outlook towards most things. I'm an unusually cheerful fella.

What I know about nihilism came from the second-hand casual use of the word, rather than what it actually meant as a philosophical position.

I initially predicted that I'd look up nihilism and realize that my impressions of it would be completely wrong and that there would be some value to it. Unfortunately, that is not the case. As a philosophical position, I strain to see how it's not at least a little garbage.1

I will extend this disrespect to other positions adjacent to them: blanket pessimism, cynicism, "everything sucks," etc. Among them nihilism is perhaps the least bad. At least I don't find the core premise disagreeable.

Nihilism, which from my understanding most commonly refers to existential nihilism, is the rejection of a meaning to life. Okay? Yeah? So?

There was probably a time where I might have been sympathetic to this. But today it just seems to me that a lot of mostly pointless rumination in western philosophy has happened over this. Might I suggest: maybe it's fine for there to be no meaning, and for anyone to figure out a new set of values to fill this void of meaning. It's okay if there's no meaning. Why do you want meaning. Say you find "meaning," now what?

Now for general pessimism. I don't quite like the optimism vs pessimism framing with the whole half-filled glass metaphor. I'd say a better phrase for what I'm describing is "negative outlook." The archetype here is someone who looked around them (or more like, looked into the polluted information environment in their screen), didn't like what they saw, and concluded "everything sucks." They stare at the abyss and flinch.

Actually this disease needs a name. Big Lifesucksism is my ideological adversary. Like the COVID virus, it is invisible and diffuse. It evades a clearly packaged catch-all descriptor like capitalism, communalism, technofascism, effective altruism, petloverism or whateverism that people often rally behind to hate on. I have seen friends lose themselves to this disease.

Big Lifesucksism has a lot of promoters and a massive decentralised grassroots network, but no leaders. It has its share of grifters (like that zerodha zero1 guy), but most people are sincere, and its promoters are mostly victims, who are in psychological pain, and inadvertently inflict psychological pain to other people via the projection of valid aversive feelings.

All of this makes Big Lifesucksism a potent adversary. There are no easy ways to counter it. Think about it:

  • The proponents of Big Lifesucksism are often in pain about real problems of modernity. In a sense, the proponents are also the victims. Attempts to reason against Big Lifesucksism are often perceived as denial of these problems, or a denial of the validity of their aversive feelings.

  • The religiously-held doctrine of Big Lifesucksism is that real problems should only ever be processed as suffering, anxiety, anger or other aversive feelings.

  • Suffering is equated with empathy. Caring for other people and wanting things to improve has only one fuel which is pain, anxiety, or anger. If these go away, it means no problem can be solved.

  • Trying to tell Big Lifesucksists that it's actually possible to process issues without holding onto suffering is a statement that is likely to induce more aversion or deepen their (validly held) pain. So actually trying to attack the root cause directly actually achieves the opposite of what one would want (which is to reduce suffering).

When I say I am optimistic person, some can interpret it as a problem denialist. That's not the case, it is more like, "everything is fixable." It forces you to look at the problem deeper, and actually admit that there's action to be taken there.

We are conscious beings, we experience things, and how we frame things to ourselves affect our behaviour, and thus our propensity to fix this. No one is immune to this. While I'm not belabouring myself to think optimistically (I don't actually choose my thoughts at all, and neither can you), trying to steer my brain cycles into being curious and understanding of even bad things makes one see that there's a lot to improve structurally and a lot to improve in this world, and that does not suck.

A common defense to lifesucksism is that this public vibe defecation of the commons with the "everything sucks" refrain actually improves things, and stirs the people into revolt. This is perhaps the most compelling argument. But it still conflates optimism with passivity, and lifesucksism with activity. I believe there are long-term negative costs and externalities to being angry and repeating and spreading the lifesucksism virus, and in my observation most people inflicted with it are far more passive than you'd assume. In fact, to drive change, to actually improve things, often requires imagining a better world and a better future. That is actually how I see the world, and it's fundamentally a positive outlook.

hall of fame

"In the 1970s hundreds of millions of people will starve to death."
"Population will inevitably and completely outstrip whatever small increases in food supplies we make... India couldn't possibly feed two hundred million more people by 1980."

Paul Ehrlich, 1968

"... it seems probable that most of the grand underlying principles have been firmly established ... An eminent physicist remarked that the future truths of physical science are to be looked for in the sixth place of decimals."

Albert A Michelson, 1894

You must in the first place know this, that the world has now grown old, and does not abide in that strength in which it formerly stood; nor has it that vigour and force which it formerly possessed.

Whatever is now born degenerates with the old age of the world itself; so that no one ought to wonder that everything begins to fail in the world, when the whole world itself is already in process of failing, and in its end.

St Cyprian of Carthage, c. 252 AD

“Our parents’ era, worse than their ancestors, bore us still worse, and soon we will give more wicked offspring.”

Horace, c. 23 BC

entry.title: Why I Write
entry.content:
One year! This site has been up for more than one year! Which is insane and doesn't make sense at all. But that is a fact. This has raised the question for me. Why do I write publicly?

But first, a time skip. About a year ago I attended an Elixir meet-up in Mumbai and I met SVS. Had a catchup meeting with him later. As I was explaining one of my projects to him, it was going poorly. I shared half naked readme, probably fumbling around in the codebase. Then he asked me quite frankly, "Why don't you WRITE about this?" This was so embarrassing. Why hadn't I done this before? He continued - Buy a domain, and write on a weekly basis. You don't have to keep it purely technical, you can write about a movie you saw also. Write regularly and keep it semi professional.

That clicked. Sometimes you just need the push. I had been writing privately for years. Sharing it with friends once in a while. Or as a part of college clubs. But to make that internal world public, that scared me. But keeping it semi professional made sense. Something in between a linkedinese speaking robot and diaristic entries, I could manage.

But still, these are only the public ones. I started writing private articles during Covid. Just to cope with it all. Why do I feel this compulsion? Eric Arthur Blair AKA George Orwell asked himself the same question some 80 years ago. Part of the essay is public. Orwell was.. well he was into language, can you believe it? The essay talks about his own motivations for writing. He generalises it to - this why writers write. There is some political stuff in it also. He was writing it as bombs were dropping on London, so makes sense.

He was a strong believer in simple, effective language mainly. He was arguing that the use of dead and complicated words was weakening the English language. Phrases or words like - at the end of the day, deserving of serious consideration, exploit, petty bourgeois. They aim at hiding stuff. Some of the phrases start out as original. But through repeated use by everyone, they become dead. They lose their original meaning. Slop basically. He named slop 80 years ago.

Here is a good example. This is the end one of my favourite poems - At Verona by Oscar Wilde:

"Curse God and die: what better hope than this?
He hath forgotten thee in all the bliss                   
Of his gold city, and eternal day"—
Nay peace: behind my prison's blinded bars
I do possess what none can take away,
My love, and all the glory of the stars.

Let us ask our friend GPT to slop-ify this -

“The proposed termination of existence, accompanied by theological denunciation, appears to constitute the sole remaining prospect. He, absorbed in the perpetual magnificence of a celestial metropolis, has ceased to retain you within his recollection."

Nevertheless, tranquillity should be maintained: beyond the visual obstructions of my confinement, I remain in possession of certain intangible assets, namely affection and the universal splendour of astronomical phenomena.”

Amazing - thank you. The point being - Good prose is like a window pane. If it does not do that, it has failed. Arrange your words with clarity and effort. Keep it simple.

It's not easy to follow his general guidelines. You have to be very alert about how you are writing. Are you dressing things up by introducing foreign words? Is this a good metaphor, or just an overused phrase? Are you overcomplicating things? And he himself admits that he has failed at the rules quite often. But that goal should also ways be in your mind. Don't lose sight of it!

But the motivations for writing, those I find quite interesting. He has 4 of them. I personally think you can also group them into two main groups: Practical and Impractical. Again totally made up, but why not. So let us categorise his reasons!

Historical Impulse

Desire to see things as they are, to find out true facts and store them up for the use of posterity.

This is pretty obvious. Write what you come across at work, describe events in your life - maybe a conference, workshop or a piece of work. This is firmly practical. And these articles I have written have proven tremendously useful. Can send them to people to show my work! Can point to something concrete while applying for programs. Especially the technical ones. They act as reference points for me! I am able to look back on my own work, think of changes to make, talk to others about it.

Even the talk at IndiaFOSS - it was only possible because the article acted as a guiding point. In fact if I followed the article line of thought even more, the talk would have been better. The process of writing such things cements concepts in your mind. And every-time you skim through the article, you are re-living that process. So speaking about things becomes easier. 11/10 would recommend.

Political purpose

Using the word ‘political’ in the widest possible sense. Desire to push the world in a certain direction, to alter other people’s idea of the kind of society that they should strive after.

This one I think is just the above one in different clothes in my opinion. Facts can be relayed, but there is always a point of view that relays them. So I will mostly ignore this. Orwell himself says this the weakest impulse in him. Putting this in the practical box. Next!

Aesthetic enthusiasm

Perception of beauty in the external world, or, on the other hand, in words and their right arrangement.

Desire to share an experience which one feels is valuable and ought not to be missed.

Would put this in the "impractical" category. Why do we like beautiful things? Something something usefulness vs beauty. But it doesn't matter. There is a misconception that non-fiction, if it's "true" it is boring. WRONG ANSWER. Our lives are stories in our heads. And if you don't tell that story well, even about real events that occurred, the point will be missed. Maybe one of my favourite Orwell lines comes for this point -

So long as I remain alive and well I shall continue to feel strongly about prose style, to love the surface of the earth, and to take pleasure in solid objects and scraps of useless information.

No use denying it. And finally

Pure Egoism

Desire to seem clever, to be talked about, to be remembered after death, to get your own back on grown-ups who snubbed you in childhood.

Aha! Now we are getting to it. Perhaps the only actual answer. I will let Orwell continue -

I had the lonely child’s habit of making up stories and holding conversations with imaginary persons, and I think from the very start my literary ambitions were mixed up with the feeling of being isolated and undervalued.

Right on. This is also firmly in the impractical box. What is even the point of pretending? You write to look special, to spite old enemies (coming soon), to lie here and there, to flatter yourself and others like you, to be mean to mostly men and some women while you are at, and to hide from the world only to find this is perhaps the best way to connect with it. Well, at least I do sometimes.

And why not? Why not write for these "bad" reasons as well? Chekhov said - "There is nothing good in this world that does not have some filth in its origin." We cannot remove these parts of ourselves. But that still explains only a part of the reason. I don't think all four of these still combine to explain why we write.

At the end of Anti-fragile or Black Swan, Taleb says this I think - We read and write for the same reasons dogs like sleeping on a particular tile. These activities will not go away. Why do I write? Ultimately I want to convey some experiences. And hope they resonate with someone. Why do we feel this need? God knows. But for now, am happy to sleep on my tile.

Post Notes

1.Orwell was born in Bengal and was in the Indian Imperial Service for five years. Someday there will be another article on Orwell and India. Another thing I can do! Make public promises.

2.This has been added later. There are so many people who have inspired me to write online. I should atleast mention them.

3.Shiela O'Malley, who writes beautifully about movies and art. She has actually allowed me to look at artists very differently. The INTENSE FEELING IN ALL CAPS technique I have just copied from her.

4.Tim Kreider was a cartoonist before he started writing and teaching. There are so many good essays he has, but this one, about practical visual effects becoming 'obsolete' is really great.

5.Joel Spolsky, perhaps the best software writers from the blogger times. Sadly he stopped writing on his site after late 2022. Hmm, wonder why?

6.Gregor Hohpe now this one I am definitely biased. He writes a lot about systems and tradeoffs. That is what I like. Think in lines, not boxes.

7.Paul Graham's writing style is something else. I find it both frustrating and inspiring.

entry.title: NASA Artemis and CLPS lunar mission updates minus the PR fluff, as all things should be
entry.content:
Artemis updates

  • On September 14, SpaceX’s Starship Super Heavy rocket reached orbit for the first time, seven years later than originally touted, continuing its slow progress in building a Lunar Starship ready to land Artemis astronauts on the Moon for NASA. As Marcia Smith reported, the orbital flight was shorter than planned but SpaceX did manage to achieve the primary goal of deploying 26 Starlink satellites in low Earth orbit. The flight does make some headway into Starship’s flight part of Artemis III, an upcoming test mission in Earth orbit before NASA attempts to land astronauts on the Moon with Artemis IV. Even there though, SpaceX’s lapses against their own promised timelines unfortunately continue since the Starship lander prototype will not fly with an environmental control and life support system. Going from there to landing humans on the Moon in six months is impossible.
Related: Milestones pending for SpaceX Starship to be a Moonship for NASA astronauts
  • Hardware preparations for Artemis III continue. NASA contracted SpaceX to downlink 4K imagery and video during the mission. To do so, SpaceX and NASA will utilize Starlink’s laser system by installing two terminal units on the crewed Orion spacecraft. In the meanwhile, technicians working for NASA connected Orion’s crew and service modules for the mission and tested said integration. Training for the four-person crew has also begun.
  • NASA released a whole set of data from April’s Artemis II lunar flyby mission, including high-resolution images and astronaut audio, a preliminary report, and more. NASA continues to call Artemis II a lunar science mission, which is not true, a distinction important for not undermining the value of and budgeting for true science missions.
  • On a connected note: NASA has called Artemis II a “global cultural moment”. The mission was certainly inspirational to many but being truly global and becoming a moment are different things altogether. Also, numbers put in context by The Planetary Society show that Artemis II was less popular than expected, assumed, or touted even in the US.
Google search trends for Artemis II are about as fleeting. On April 7 — the day after the mission’s crew flew around the farside of the Moon — the Masters Tournament held more search interest, despite not actually beginning for another two days. The tournament would go on to be more popular on Google overall.
  • First reported by Ars Technica and later confirmed by NASA administrator Jared Isaacman in an internal memo to employees, the agency has decided to use a simpler version of the Axiom-Space-provided AxEMU spacesuit for Artemis IV lunar surface mission. The development of this ‘Sortie Suit’ with relaxed requirements is intended to accelerate the developmental pace against constantly slipping timelines for the lunar suit.
  • The University of Münster, German Space Agency, NASA, and Intuitive Machines are collaborating to develop an automated pipeline for generating 3D lunar mapping products from high-resolution imagery taken by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO). This is useful for advanced mission planning, such as for selecting safe landing regions and optimal surface traverses.
  • ESA’s latest round of its Pangaea campaign to train astronauts in geology again has one NASA astronaut onboard, Jasmin Moghbeli.
  • The US-led Artemis Accords, presented as a non-binding avenue of cooperative lunar exploration, now has over 75 signee nations, with Djibouti, Albania, Croatia, Côte d’Ivoire, and San Marino being the newest signatories. In the meanwhile, NASA’s administrator asked international partners to only provide “good deals” while the agency itself cancelled the NASA-led Gateway international lunar habitat earlier this year wherein partners had not just significant but fundamental contributions. Also, the US President recently claimed the Moon to be American territory, which went completely unreported much less critiqued by many western space and technology media outlets who otherwise pounce to cover equivalent statements by officials on the other side of the world. Between statements like these and Gateway’s cancellation, it’s never been more clear that the Artemis Accords unfortunately has little to no bearing on preserving—much less flourishing—international partnerships in the Artemis program.

CLPS updates

  • Considering the roughly yearly launch cadence intended for Firefly’s upcoming Moon landing missions part of NASA’s CLPS program—Blue Ghost the second, third, fourth, and fifth—as well as the company’s desire for more landing contracts as part of NASA’s Moonbase plans, Firefly completed building a new cleanroom facility which is four times larger than the one used to assemble the first Blue Ghost lander, which last year successfully soft landed on the Moon for the US this century.
  • Relatedly, NASA’s retroreflector payload mounted on Firefly’s first Blue Ghost CLPS lunar lander was used to successfully reflect laser signals by multiple ranging observatories in Europe and the US. In the future, having multiple retroreflectors on the surface can aid navigation for orbital and incoming surface spacecraft. Also, data from Blue Ghost’s SCALPSS payload which imaged surface dust kickup and disturbances caused by the lander’s engine plumes has been put up on NASA’s Planetary Data System archive. Simeon Schmauß made a cool timelapse video of the lunar surface view of SCALPSS from beneath the lander.
  • NASA selected three more science instruments to be delivered to different, payload-relevant areas on the Moon on as-yet-unspecified CLPS landers.
  • NASA announced a $38 million contract to Modulate Space Cooperation for demonstrating lunar surface 5G and WiFi-6 communications by 2028. The release doesn’t mention any lander but a CLPS delivery seems likely. The agency is also continuing to fund other lunar engineering projects, such as research on plastic made from lunar soil simulants and terrestrial bacteria and better electrical grounding for future astronauts near landers.

More Moon

  • Other recent Moon mission briefings
    • Moon Monday #292: An obsessively linked rundown of recent global lunar exploration and cooperation updates
    • China is building a lunar navigation and communications network. Lasers shine again in latest demonstration.
    • Moon Monday #287: Mission updates from China, the US, Europe, and Japan
  • Lunar conferences I will be at:
    • Thailand’s national space agency is hosting the 10th Global Moon Village Workshop & Symposium in the last week of October. Right after it takes place the Thailand Space Expo.
    • China is once again hosting a symposium on lunar sample research at the University of Hong Kong in November 3rd week, with the location being selected to enable ease of access for international participants like the last time. Last year’s symposium saw an amazing set of lunar science updates. I’m excited to see and cover what’s in store this time.
    • Are you or your friends or colleagues planning to attend any of these conferences? If so, let’s meet and chat all things space and science. Please write to me.

Many thanks to Open Lunar Foundation and Dany Waller for sponsoring Moon Monday. If you too appreciate my efforts to bring you this curated community resource on global lunar exploration for free, and without ads, kindly support my independent writing as it’s purely reader-funded. I don’t use AI to write a single word and cite everything.

Support Moon Monday 🌙

It feels like a major life turn after 35, even though I thought 35 was like half-life. I haven’t crossed the second half-life yet. I think there are a couple more years until the second half-life, but it still feels like a big turn after 35. I didn’t think much about 45, but this one feels big.

Anyway, this year has been good, I think. Overall, I’ve been working hard and smart at the same time, focusing on what I call being nice to my future self, in a way that my future self feels good. That includes working out today so my future self is healthy, saving a bit today so my future self is wealthy, and building relationships today so my future self is happy. Things like that. I’m not overly focusing on my future self, but not ignoring him either.

It’s kind of about building or doing things for my current self while also helping my future self. It also kind of works on a day to day basis. Like, I try to sleep well so my tomorrow is better. I try to eat well so my tomorrow is better. I try to finish one extra task so tomorrow is better. Things like that. Small things. That’s been the idea of this year, and I think I’ve done well in the shorter term. But in the longer term, I still have to see the results.

We are doing okay as a family. We are enjoying our parenting. Echo is getting older and older. It’s not easy to watch him get old, but that’s happening. Paatu has become an adult, but she still thinks she’s the youngest one. Uma is actually the youngest one, but she acts like a grown-up.

Anju and I are trying to figure out some things together. Generally, both my parents and Anju’s are getting old. So we’re seeing how to handle that, how to manage that along with our currently growing responsibilities at home, with the home and kids. I think we are doing okay overall. In terms of money, we are living comfortably and saving, though I would like to save a bit more than usual, given how the economy is going. We’re also trying to figure out how to manage our savings and investments better in the current situations.

I have been trying to take time out to meet friends this year. I have been quite successful. It’s been great; I want to keep doing that. I’m also very grateful to have them in my life.

I don’t think the future will be easy in terms of work or time. I can only say that I can prepare myself for it now that I know it’s going to be tough.

I’ve been quite healthy compared to last year. Anju also has been quite okay. I’ve settled down to a rhythm in terms of exercises and how my schedule is organized around that, and I’m paying attention to my health. So that way, it has been good.

In terms of work, I’ve been doing well. I’ve been working hard and smart, as I said before, but I’m also trying a lot of different things to stay engaged in this new work world.

I think I’ve been overworking a bit this year, which I’ll probably reduce a bit next year. But it’s been good; only because the teams have been good to me, and the work has been good, interesting, and challenging. Otherwise, I think it would have gotten to me by now.

That is all. Overall, it’s been a good year.

Hopefully, next year will be great because I have big plans, especially for motorcycling.

Hopefully, I’ll be able to write about it in detail soon, probably by December. I should have a plan for the ride worked out by then; that’s a big dream and target for next year. Some friends are hopefully joining me. Let’s see how it goes.

Otherwise, I’m grateful for the year. I hope to do better next year. Thank you and love you.

entry.title: Weeknote October 6 - October 12 2026
entry.content:
Somehow every conversation I have with people always seems to eventually lead to AI.

I am not a huge fan of the way closed source AI companies have gone about in training their AI models, or the fact that they have access to your prompts they are able to steal anything you work on.

I also see and understand the excitement people have. It's a weird time.

I had sort of a technical pre-screener online interview with a company who had me debug issues related to an AI wrapper they are supplying. The byline was that these are the types of production issues you will be working on. 5 issues, 6 mins per issue debugging AI slop code by using AI slop because we are meat proxies.

It made me feel a type of disdain for the money men who are so gung ho about using this technology, and also for how willingly our field accepted being code-cuckolds. This might seem like a rant, old man yelling at clouds or what not, but seriously this is what CS is going to be?

AI writes the code, AI reviews the code, AI suggests PR edits, AI merges the code, but the person liable is the human. Such non sense.

Now, I am not above the slop. It is useful to get velocity, but the promise of doing less work and having time for the important stuff has been a lie. Now the unrealistic expectations of being 10000X developer has arrived.

And the ones who are supplying this Slop Juice are laughing their way to the bank.

I use AI to do boring stuff which I don't want to do, like a concierge. I have apply to jobs for me, write Cover Letters that make it seem like I have drank the Kool-Aid, because so many people have.

So that's been my week, giving ai slop assessments for ai slop companies. Meh.

Besides that I was sick all week. I have had a little bit of a cold and cough. I haven't slept properly in 3 days either. I am just moving by drinking enough white monster to keep myself alert and awake.

Workouts are going fine but I've not been able to go spar because I don't want the other people i interact with to catch my cold.

My health improved by the weekend and I met a couple of my friends to enjoy some really good chicken in Bangalore at an underrated eatery which I intend to gatekeep and have it remain a hidden gem. Sometimes when you haven't eaten all day the best thing in the world is a hot chicken lollipop curry with thin chapatis , egg rice, chicken kababs and other items shared with friends and a laugh.

My niece is getting to be a chatterbox in the way one year olds are. Her constant babbling is a fun time because we all have our own opinions about what she's saying. She can communicate now, she calls dogs bow bow and says bye. It's interesting watching someone develop intelligence like this.

So good days and bad days are just happening and so goes another week.

entry.title: bad taste bathrooms
entry.content:
Disclaimer: if you can't handle bathroom pictures, click away. They are a bit dank, but nothing too horrifying.

Where does bad taste come from?

I see what I consider bad taste everywhere around me. Most of it is boringly bad. A random wardrobe that belongs in a cheap 2BHK rental right outside the washroom of a Third Wave Coffee outlet (which, in another turn of bad taste, serves second-wave coffee). I am in fact sitting in this outlet as I write this. The table is too tall, and the cappuccino's straw is at the level of my nostrils. Perhaps this coffee is meant to be snorted, and not tasted.

Bathrooms with bad taste are a lot less boring. They are either totally neglected or overthought. A recent one I witnessed was in Konark, a 1985 outlet that's been serving solid food for three generations. They seemed to have had some kind of renovation a few years ago, as the interiors do not evoke 1985. More like 2018. The washroom had an interesting design. It's a small square with all three corners occupied by a urinal, an Indian toilet and a western commode.

I wonder how this came to be. Perhaps, there was only the Indian toilet to begin with, and someone thought that it would be fantastic to give consumers a preferred mode of excretion.

It's not much better in newfangled posh restaurants. I was in Boteco the other day, a fairly expensive Brazilian restaurant, right under the BlackRock office. In the table next to mine was a classic uncle who had the appearance of someone named Nagaraj Byregowda sitting across two Koreans, all in suits. And he was speaking and gesturing to them in fluent Korean. The restaurant was papered with the typical piss-yellow overly ornate AI slop art.

The bathroom is in a narrow passage, near a corner that also leads into the kitchen. People kept jamming themselves up against the waiters, while trying to get to the bathroom, only to realise that it's engaged. Inside, was some kind of faux-tokyo cypberpunk aesthetic that was nothing like the rest of the place. Black tiles, black commode, incense. No one lit it and there was no ventilation, so it smelled a bit farty. There was an emergency box with a wine bottle in it, and a sticker on it, which was some joke that I can't quite remember about breaking the glass in case of an emergency.

The worst part was the tap. I didn't take a picture because I was already a bit irked, but I found a pictures online of this abomination called a "joystick mixer."

It looks unassuming, but it took me two minutes to figure out how to turn on the damn thing. It's not particularly high on pressure either. It appeared to be a little annoying to clean for the staff, and there was already a bunch of municipal hard water sediment around the part where the water flows. Maybe that's why the "joystick" itself was so creaky and stiff, requiring a lot of force. Just looking at it, can you guess how to turn it on? How do you control the force?

What likely happened here is that some interior designer sold a vision of luxury and sleekness to whoever operates the restaurant. It's definitely a bathroom that would look much better in pictures.

Here's the thing though. In the large, I'm not too bothered about this. I think "bad taste" is a mostly unavoidable phenomenon in today's society. It happens when economic growth, technology, and creation of wealth outpaces culture, or specifically, knowledge of what feels like the right fit for human needs. Culture diffuses a lot more slowly, it can't handle the kind of acceleration that we see in technology or GDP. If we want to accelerate "good culture," it's important to figure out how to ground people and make them more observant of the world we live in.

entry.title: Design As Art
entry.content:
I got a good deal on a hardcover copy of Walter Isaacson's Steve Jobs biography, so I decided to atone for this techbro cliché by also purchasing this sleek, overpriced paperback of Bruno Munari's Design As Art (1966). Flipping through the pages, I saw a lot of interesting images and studies, and I thought I'd probably learn a thing or two from this book.

Bruno Munari is an artist and designer, and I'm being somewhat reductionist here. He's clearly had his fingers in a lot of fields. He came up as an artist in fascist Italy, and initially associated himself with the futurist art movement. But over time, especially after the war he distanced himself from all that and became more of an industrial designer type of guy with a relatively progressive outlook.

This book has no cohesion and the title is totally inaccurate. Turns out this is an English translation, and the original title of Arte come mestiere is better translated as something like "Art as trade" which maybe is better, but still inaccurate. Maybe a good title for this today might just be "Bruno Munari's Design Blog."

If Munari were alive today, he would have been a blogging God. While this book is not high on insights, it's extremely sharp-witted, fast-flowing, and entertaining. Just look at this excerpt from "Fancy Goods":

‘You’re always so full of ideas. Give me an idea for a Christmas present, not one of the ordinary things you find in the usual shops.’

How was I to set about it? Well, first of all I had to get an idea of what my lady friend meant by ordinary things. I did a tour of the gift shops that sell fancy goods, just to see what they had in stock.

In one shop I see a brass boot, size 25 (approx.). ‘I’ll have a pair of those,’ I say. ‘We have only one, sir.’ ‘What can I do with one boot?’ ‘It is not a boot to wear on the foot, sir. It is a boot to keep umbrellas in,’ the assistant explains, smiling patiently as one would at a madman. I am greatly embarrassed by this gaffe, and leave the shop at once, nearly tripping over a marble cat decorated with floral reliefs and serving as a doorstop. I am beginning to learn.

As I stand indecisively outside the shop my glance happens to light on a copper frying-pan hanging on the wall. It is not meant to be used as a frying-pan, of course, because it has clock-hands attached and numbers from one to twelve. Ah… then it is a clock. It is in the shape of a frying-pan because it is for the kitchen. And a clock for the lavatory? [...]

He goes on listing examples like this for a couple more pages, really rubbing in the ridiculousness of it all.

[...] A photo-frame like a pocket watch, scissors like a flamingo, a salt-cellar like a wheelbarrow with a spoon like a shovel. A dish for fish shaped like a fish, a dish for pig’s foot shaped like a pig’s foot, a tureen for tomato soup shaped like soup. A hammer like a fish, a fish like a hammer, a cheese-dish in the form of a sitting hen, a thermos flask for ice, shaped like a football.

A dish for fruit in the shape of a leaf, an old wooden cradle for use as a magazine rack…

These are certainly not objects produced by designers, for designers do not have such raging imaginations. They confine themselves to making candlesticks that look like candlesticks. But look, what have we here? An antique gun hung on the wall as a hatstand, with a row of hooks soldered along the barrel. Or an enormous key with smaller hooks, for hanging real keys on. A cigarette lighter in the shape of a revolver, a revolver in the shape of a cigarette lighter. [... this goes on for a while longer]

By this time my head is spinning and I don’t know for sure whether what I am seeing is really there. I don’t know whether to put my cigarette ash into someone’s hand or to screw the light-bulb into the soup-tureen. What on earth can I say to my lady friend? If we have gone this far at Christmas, where will we be at carnival time?

However, I do say something. I say, let’s buy a pipe that is really a pipe, let’s fill it with real tobacco, light a match that looks like a match and works like a match, and apply it to the pipe-pipe. Let us have a cup of coffee in a cuplike cup on a table-table near our chairlike chair, and read a good book-book. And my friend gets all upset. She climbs into her Mini tarted up to look like a Cadillac and roars off into the mist, sounding like a Ferrari.

Every chapter reads roughly like a blog post, and there's not a clear thing connecting each chapter, nor is there much of a broader point to be made. My takeaways from this book are:

  • Art has lost its connection with the public. Designers are planners with aesthetic sense, and they must reconnect with people through everyday objects (this is pretty much the only thing that's relevant to the book title, and is the focus of the earlier chapters).

  • Munari strongly believes that function must dictate form. He divides the world into designers and stylists, and the latter care about aesthetic flourishes only in isolation (to match the fashions of the time).

  • Good design should take inspiration from nature, but not through mere imitation. The designer must observe and understand the mechanisms for why things in nature work, and smartly incorporate those mechanisms and affordances in designs.

The book divides itself into four categories: Design As Art, Visual Design, Graphic Design, Industrial Design, and Research Design. The chapters in Industrial Design is where Munari is at his best.

In the spirit of treating this book like a blog, let me recommend some of my favourite Munari posts:

Children's Books. Munari talks through his thought process for writing books for children, and criticises how books are often designed to make parents feel good, rather than actually engage with children.

[The publisher] thinks that it is not children who buy books. They are bought by grown-ups who give them as presents not so much to amuse the child as to cut a (sometimes coldly calculated) dash with the parents. A book must therefore be expensive, the illustrations must use every colour in the rainbow, but apart from that it doesn’t matter even if they are ugly. A child won’t know the difference because he’s just a little nincompoop. The great thing is to make a good impression.

Wear and Tear. A meditation on when and how wear and tear must inform the design of things.

What could be more utterly wrongheaded than the heel of a shoe? Upon this we put the whole weight of our bodies while standing or walking. As soon as we actually use these heels we destroy them, yet we obstinately persist in putting identical heels back on again. These are heels made to be admired in shop windows, while the shoes are as useless and as stationary as pieces of sculpture. Certain children’s shoes are now made with rounded heels, and start out in the shape that wear will reduce them to anyway. But this is impossible for grown-ups. Such shoes wouldn’t sell. They’re not dignified.

Orange, Peas and Rose. A bizarre joke chapter, where Munari describes objects of nature as though they were a product designed by someone. It really puts across Munari's careful and attentive observations on the nature of things.

Orange

This object is made up of a series of modular containers shaped very much like the segments of an orange and arranged in a circle around a vertical axis. Each container or section has its straight side flush with the axis and its curved side turned outwards. In this way the sum of their curved sides forms a globe, a rough sphere.

All these sections are packed together in a container that is quite distinctive both as to its material and its colour. Its outside surface is fairly hard, but it has a soft internal lining that serves as padding between the outer surface and the sections packed inside. The material is in origin all of the same type, but it is suitably differentiated according to its function.

Each section or container consists of an envelope of plastic-like material large enough to contain the juice but easy to handle during the dismemberment of the global form. The sections are attached to one another by a very weak, though adequate, adhesive. The outer or packing container, following the growing tendency of today, is not returnable and may be thrown away.

A Piece of Travelling Sculpture. This is a commentary on the design of cars of that time. It has aged finely.

Either we ought to apply aesthetic criteria to everything, or forget them completely. Why do we criticize the ‘line’ of a mudguard but never think of questioning the tread of a tyre? Did you ever hear of anyone refusing to buy a tyre because its design didn’t go with his waistcoat? No, because a car is part machine and part drawing-room. Have you heard how these styling experts talk? Just listen to them: ‘giving the interior a more intimate character… an inspired model… a delicious harmony of colours… a new, more slender line… an utterly personal interpretation… a real jewel’, etc. Isn’t this the kind of talk you expect to hear in a couturier’s salon? And of course the word salon is actually used for exhibitions of new cars. And what do you think these gentlemen ought to be talking about? They should be discussing the real problems, aside from matters of aesthetics and personal taste and the art of sculpturing forms. Their designs should be based on statistics and lab tests, on the ceaseless study of form, function and cost.

And That's Not All... This is a commentary on a designer's never-ending obsession with chairs. He presents the futility of perfecting the chair effectively: with few words, and lots of delightful illustrations of chairs. There's seven pages of chair images.

An Arrow Can Lose Its Feathers but Not Its Point. He is quite literal about it. He shows how the humble arrow sign started out as an actual image of an arrow, and over time became abstract, until what remained is only the bare essence of what it is trying to convey.

There's a short appendix called "The Machines of My Childhood (1924)" where he describes an old floating watermill he poked at as a child. He goes back to look for that machine, and sees that it is gone.

With that, the book ends abruptly, and as will this note.

entry.title: children
entry.content:
Some people dislike children. Others viscerally love them. I don't have strong feelings. I am perhaps not exposed to them enough to be cornered into either camp.

When I see children show up in any social setting, it's often one surrounded by many other adults. The child becomes the center of attention with all the peekiweekies, whistles, claps and the like, and I thus keep to myself. There's plenty enough stimulation for the child to deal with.

For now, I remain deep in the throes of the grown-up world, formed of quarter- and mid-life crises, corporate intrigue, large legible ambitions, self help thinking, and copious amounts of hyper-self-awareness.

That said, I suspect that I'd love children.

I still have memories of what it was like to be of the ungrown class. There were downsides of course. For one, I remember being quite a bit stupider than I am now. As a child, whenever my family tried to pass a level-crossing, I used to quite sincerely get concerned about a train hitting our car, and I used to admonish my parents for trying to attempt such an endangering manoeuver. Turn around, I'd say. Find a way to go around the railway track. This stupidity is why I never yearn to become a child again. Because children are so mentally undercooked, adults feel entitled to go all authoritarian on them, and with the wrong adults (as has been the case in a lot of my childhood encounters with grown-ups), it can be a world of wretchedness.

However there were many upsides. There's a clean simplicity to a child's mind and emotions. Children are dreamy, frenetic, and hooked deeply into the present moment. They do not think about thoughts about their thoughts regarding an imagined hypothetical and then drown themselves in a prolonged ennui. The world is new to them, low on preconceptions, and free of complex desires. There's no gunk or deep-seated beliefs to fight when they have to update their representation and understanding of the world.

Their emotions are naturally swift, strong, and yet fleeting, like bright flashes of primary colour, quite unlike the wistfully dull and complex textures of grey, olive, and sepia-tone world of grown-up emotions.

There's also no two ways about it—children are cute—and also comically tiny and ill-proportioned. They are socially accepted, or rather, socially welcomed idiots (if you are a child reading this, I'm sorry. But this is objectively true). Their very existence is a form of visual comedy, and their motions evoke slapstick. We cut them slack because they just got here.

Watching a thing grow and unfold into something can be insightful. Their learning rate is fantastically high due to them not having experienced the most basic things, and it can be quite satisfying seeing them strain their faces with confusion and then suddenly get something, all in real time.

Despite being little blockheads, they are far more radiant than most adults and full of aura. There's a certain balance and correctness to the simple thinking that's prior to the formation of concepts that obscure the clarity of experience, and grown-ups should take more notes from them. As we grow older we learn to ignore the fantastic complexity of nature and the institutions that surround us, so that we can focus on our narrow grown-up matters. A child does not discern between what should be ignored and what should one make sense of.

A conversation with a child often reveals how shallow our understanding of just about anything is. What is wall made of? Why should my socks match? Why is the moon following us? Why do I have to do [what I am being forced to do]? How did the first person get chicken-pox? Why is that guy fat? How come I have two eyes, but just one picture? Can you tell me what things are? Why do ceiling fans have only three blades? Are you sure this is not a dream? Are dogs left-pawed or right-pawed?

Most adults would bumble a rather imprecise answer to most of these questions.

Meanwhile adults have the most inane, dull questions for children. What do you want to be when you grow up? Do you remember me? Have you been a good boy? Repeat that rhyme for me. Tell me what they taught you at school today?

School. It is a pipeline where children are taught to obey, and answer questions rather than ask them, and then they become grown-ups who will ask these inane questions to the next generation of children again.

Or you could not be a typical grown up. The loss of radiance is not inevitable. You could see the world anew, one prior to the concepts that were drilled in your head.

entry.title: Trying to fill my well again
entry.content:
On losing confidence and making things for myself again.

Last week I spectacularly stammered my way through a conversation at work. The frustrating part was, this was something I had researched and worked on for weeks. Something I should have been able to explain in my sleep. But the moment I joined the Slack huddle, the words scattered, tumbling out of my mouth and onto the floor.

I have been feeling a serious loss of confidence over the last few months. I have spent a large part of my time over the last two years building successful things and watching them progress in the world and propagate a belief system I hold. But for all the plaudits the work received, it never truly felt mine.

The work used to go out, and people were excited, even ecstatic, about it; but my well still sat empty.

I am proud of these things! But they did not give me the same feeling I get when doing something just for myself. Like a piece of writing, which I have been doing more of recently. Or a project I poured my heart into a while ago. I keep finding joy in the things I did for myself, long after they have been completed.

A few weeks ago, in a long conversation with a very dear friend and fellow artist, we decided to read The Artist’s Way by Julia Cameron together. Another friend recommended this to me nearly six years ago, and it has been on my radar since, but I just never picked it up.

The current crisis of confidence pushed me into reading it. Over the last week or so, I have been working through the chapters, getting a feel for the book. Like every other book in this genre, it starts with a few detailed, slightly long, and somewhat praise-y pages on why “this” is the best method yet. It also has a few too many references to God for my belief system’s liking.

But as I read through and learn more about the intention behind the book, it has aligned well with me. I consider myself an artist, and everyone around me one too. Maybe repeating it for twelve weeks will finally make me believe it.

The opening chapters ask for something specific. Show up for the next twelve weeks and do the two basic tools the book is built on: three morning pages every day and one artist date every week, trusting that the wanting to create counts on its own.

A good chunk of the early chapters is about the inner critic, the voice that has been running commentary in my head for months now, and the book asks you to catch it and shut it down before it gets a vote. After months of my well feeling empty, a book with an entire idea built around filling the well back up felt aimed directly at me.

This morning I did my first-ever morning pages. Three pages longhand before anything else, no editing, no rereading (I really wanted to). The thing I am most proud of is that I only got distracted twice during those 28 minutes. I am hopeful and skeptical in equal measure, trying to respect the wisdom of the book and keep going. My one worry is how this sits alongside all the other writing in my life.

Honestly, I am out of other ideas too. I want to feel good about the work I create and bring into this world, and this book is the best plan I have right now.

The artist dates are something I am genuinely looking forward to. Something I do for myself anyway, but now it has a name. Hoping it gives my photography more dedicated time, instead of the spare scraps of attention it has been surviving on.

As I wrap up this blog, I feel an urge to keep creating and to pay close attention to the art around me. I am reminded that art is especially necessary now, when those in power are willing to shut down the country’s capital and fundamental institutions are crumbling. Art can help hold those in power to account. So the morning pages continue tomorrow.

entry.title: How petting became my love language
entry.content:
I come from Malegaon, a small town near Nashik. My house was located in a very prominent lane. Whenever I stepped outside the house, every few steps, I would come across a familiar face. I must say that the lane was very lively. But it also carried gossip in the air. For me, the whole lane was full of activities like playing, snacking, and chatting at the katta. I still cannot believe I spent my whole childhood in that lane

When I shifted to Mumbai for further studies, I remember being amazed by the huge crowd around me but being unable to find any familiar faces among them. The streets themselves felt alien, and it was hard for me to find the comfort and belongingness I knew. I would walk with loneliness in my heart

I do have social anxiety, so it’s very hard for me to make friends easily. I masked it well enough to let only a hint of it escape from within me. The newness of the city added to it. I spent many years in Mumbai carrying that feeling inside me until one day, I stopped and started observing the things around me. I started connecting with things that were easy to find, like trees and birds (in this case, mostly crows, as Mumbai is full of them). My eyes were especially drawn to street dogs, as I felt we were carrying similar feelings.

I remember being hesitant to pet a street dog initially. But once I started, I never stopped. Now, no matter which city I am in, I know I won't feel lonely. Seeing them on the street gives me immediate comfort. Sometimes I get affection from them, sometimes I get solidarity from them. I always thank them for their existence and feel sorry for the pain we humans have caused them.

So, this has become my habit, I always look for street dogs. They have taught me something very important, love should flow freely and cannot be limited to a particular family. Love should be easy to find. It doesn't have a particular face. Hence one of my love languages is petting

entry.title: you need alternative markers of progress
entry.content:
Weight loss and other stuff

I have been on a weightloss journey since December of last year and I am planning to write a blog about what worked, what didn't, etc. But today a comment by my dear mother made me think that I need to put this down because it is important.

Body shaming is a casual occurance in my household. It comes as easy as breathing to people who feel that providing such comments is motivating. I know that it is the same in most Indian families where the expectation is to look a certain way despite eating food which doesn't really suit your nutritional goals.

I suffer with body dysmorphia, it is a horrible to not be comfortable in your own skin, I am sure some of you can relate to wearing clothes which are overly baggy, wear sweaters or hoodies in sweltering heat.

When I was much younger and dumber I did stupid things to get lean or get muscular because I thought it would make me seem more attractive. It is super shallow, but when you feel like an ugly duckling all your life you will take whatever motivation you can get. So I did things like OMAD (a diet where you eat your required calories in one sitting for one meal and then fast for the rest of the 23 hours), Keto, intermittent fasting, etc.

All of this didn't really address the core issues which I had which was a deep depression (yay). I sought comfort in binge eating and hence the weight gain. I would definitely lose weight with the diet but it would not be sustainable and I would be back to my usual habits within a few months.

Now that I have the vocabulary for my eating habits and I know my behaviours I am able to manage my weight. I intend to follow this for the rest of my life.

This gets me to the crux of why I made this post. Today evening after dinner my mother made a comment saying that while she can see that I have lost weight, she wishes that I had a flat stomach with the X shape physique.

If I was younger and not as well adjusted I would take that comment to heart and it would ruin my night, but since being well regulated I decided to tell her that there are other markers of progress which will definitely not show up on my body, and expecting me to look like someone she watches drop lies and misinfo on youtube is super unrealistic.

Seriously I have no idea why so many celebritries in India have a difficult time admitting that they go to the gym every day, take whey protein, creatine and steroids or have gone under the knife to look a certain way. It would really take the pressure off young women and men.

I am not sure which person has spread the misinfo about how drinking whey protein and creatine causes kidney failures or heart attacks but I have heard this story a hundred times from people who don't know any better but won't admit it (there is always some distant relative who has a friend who has a son who dropped dead in gym with whey protein dribbling out of his mouth and his heart exploded or whatever fearmongering they need to at that moment).

Watch any Indian celeb get asked about anything to do with protein or their fitness and you will see them basically get stunlocked like a deer in headlights before the programming in their heads takes over for their interviews where they will always extol the virtues of daal, chawal and ghee (obviously to seem relatable to the working class people while throwing away food casually which would probably bankrupt most households), meanwhile I can see that they are dropping some serious currency on TRT and HGH to stay that built in their 50s to 60s.

Necessity of Alternative Markers of progress

If you are struggling with your weight I know firsthand the true, unbridled self hatred while looking at yourself in the mirror and avoiding taking pictures. I am there with you and it sucks. I don't have pictures of myself from some of the worst years of my life which is also a blessing in disguise so silver lining I guess.

If you are putting in the effort to go to the gym or thinking about it, you will need a baseline that is not just how wide your waist is or how you look in the nude.

Here is the homework assignment for this one (A first for this blog for sure):

  • Write down your current weight in a diary.

  • Do a plank and a start a timer and see how long you last. If a plain plank is difficult do a side plank. If you feel like your knees are buckling then just do the plank with your knees touching the ground. It's about establishing the baseline. note down the time and what type of plank you did.

  • Do a pushup, see how many you can do, again if you have trouble make it as easy as you need to. Start with a wall pushup if you have to. Note that shit down same as above.

  • Lot of people struggle with pullups, see if you can do one, if you can't just run a timer and see how long you can do a deadhang. Note it down.

If you are going to the gym by the end of the month I can gurantee that the values you have written down will increase even marginally, If you can't do a pushup at all, you will be doing at least one knee pushup by the end of the month, if you have a 10 second dead hang it will go up to 30, and so on and so forth and what have you.

It is obvious, but it needs to be said because when you are deep in self hatred and self doubt you will need to turn to these things. The goal can be to look a certain way, but the progress to a goal weight is never linear and sometimes the weighing scale is not the whole story.

But whatever progress that you make can be measured and that is as simple as just doing things your body was never capable of doing before.

I completed a 15 km run today, back in December I would get winded by a walk. I was fighting and I was strong but I had no gas tank and now I do.

That does not show up on my body, neither does the 100 kg deadlift I did to check what my max deadlift was. I was not able to do even a single pullup back in December because I was a thick boy and it's significantly harder thing to pull up a 100 kg person compared to 85 and now I can do 10 easily.

These are markers of progress, some person who doesn't know me can easily think that I am out of shape or look like a bloated homunculus who should be locked inside a dark room with the key lost, and that's not true. Opinions are like assholes everyone has one, and indian familes love giving unsolicited opinions for free.

A marker of progress can also be decreasing the amount of times you are eating unhealthy food at restaurants. That can mean eliminating or decreasing eating outside as much or altogether or choosing to eat healthier food. It can be just going on a hike with friends when you felt exhausted after a short walk.

Conclusion

It is easy to have self-hatred and getting out of it is difficult. Have markers which you can celebrate, because that positive feedback makes a difference in showing up to the gym, to work, even showing up in relationships (your cat will hiss at you initially, but with some time and treats it will be purring on your lap by the end of the month)

Obvious stuff but it's better than being stuck at the bottom of a hole.

entry.title: Weekly Notes 41/2026
entry.content:
This week was good. I got back to my routine after two weeks of travel and a hectic schedule. Work is progressing well; I did two P.T. sessions, a game, and a run walk. I am still away from a five day active week. But I think I am consistently reaching three to four day active weeks, which isn’t bad. We are in the last quarter of the year (actual year?), I have lots of things to close before the year ends. I think it’s going to be a hectic but fruitful year end.

  • I have been building many of my projects in public for a long time, but not all my work can be public, and not every team I work with works that way. Still, I’ve found a pattern that works for most teams and for me: something like open office hours, except we’re all working. I call it Katte – The Open Desk. We meet online at a specific time, in one or two hour blocks, ideally with 2 to 8 people, and work together or separately, talking only when it helps. It’s mainly meant for teams, but it can also work with strangers as a form of accountability. This week I documented it.
  • A friend, Bharathi, at NPTEL/CODE turned 50. It seems like she is just getting started, even after achieving so much. She is such an inspiration to me.
  • I attended a lecture by Peggy Mohan at APU today. It was brilliant and also fun. She is such a brilliant storyteller.
  • We are making great progress at Dristi V2. The last two weeks were spent designing. It’s been build and build week. The next few weeks will be the same, I guess. Once it reaches some stage, I will share more details.
  • Uthara and Dave from BuzzWomen wrote a book, The Buzz Way, covering how they work. Congratulations, Uthara and Dave.
  • Tomorrow, October 10th, is a big deal; I am guessing based on how far the Delhi police will go to prevent the peaceful protests. If they were this proactive in general, Delhi wouldn’t have become the crime capital. I am very optimistic about the protests; they are going to be large, effective, and, above all, peaceful.
  • NCF is 30 years old now. They are celebrating with lots of programming; attend if you can. Aleph Alpha has built Savanna, a model factory that implements the entire training pipeline in code so that models can be built collaboratively. They have also released their open-weights model, Kolibri. I haven’t tried it yet, but it looks interesting. I came across RoadStr, decentralized road-event reporting using Nostr and MeshCore. Web and Android. It’s very close to the project I had proposed at FOSSHack/2026. I am trying it in a browser now. I will definitely try it on OSMAnd using their plugin. I need to see if I can collect historical data for a specific location for research. Otherwise, it looks great. I am also studying and exploring the Reticulum Network. It seems useful and stable, especially when the bandwidth needs are small.
